lessons.title: 1.1 What Is Artificial Intelligence?
lessons.html:
📖 What Is Artificial Intelligence?
Software that learns patterns from data instead of following rules someone wrote.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

What Is Artificial Intelligence?

What Is Artificial Intelligence? is the focus of this Introduction to AI and Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to explain how AI and cybersecurity protect people, data, and systems.

artificial intelligence

Computer systems designed to perform tasks associated with human intelligence.

cybersecurity

Protection of systems, networks, and data from digital threats.

threat

A circumstance or actor capable of causing harm.

Artificial intelligence is the branch of computing concerned with systems that perform tasks normally requiring human judgement: recognising images, understanding language, spotting patterns, making predictions.

Traditional software follows rules a programmer wrote. AI systems infer their rules from examples. That difference is why AI is useful in security — attackers change their methods faster than anyone can write rules for them.

Key points

  • AI is the broad field; machine learning is the main technique within it.
  • Rule-based software is told what to do; ML systems learn from labelled examples.
  • AI needs data. Poor or biased training data produces poor, biased results.
  • AI produces probabilities, not certainties — it can be confidently wrong.
  • Narrow AI does one task well; general AI does not exist today.
  • In security, AI supports human analysts rather than replacing them.

Example

A rule-based spam filter blocks messages containing “free money”. Attackers write “frëe m0ney” and get through. A trained model looks at hundreds of signals at once — sender history, link structure, wording patterns — and still flags it.

Why this matters

Every AI topic later in this course rests on this distinction. Knowing that a model outputs a probability, not a verdict, is what stops an analyst from trusting a tool blindly.

lessons.title: 1.2 What Is Cybersecurity?
lessons.html:
📖 What Is Cybersecurity?
Protecting systems, networks and data from unauthorised access, damage or disruption.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

What Is Cybersecurity?

What Is Cybersecurity? is the focus of this Introduction to AI and Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to explain how AI and cybersecurity protect people, data, and systems.

artificial intelligence

Computer systems designed to perform tasks associated with human intelligence.

cybersecurity

Protection of systems, networks, and data from digital threats.

threat

A circumstance or actor capable of causing harm.

Cybersecurity is the practice of defending computers, networks, applications and data against attack. It covers technology, processes and people — and people are usually the weakest of the three.

The discipline is organised around three goals, known as the CIA triad: keeping data confidential, keeping it accurate, and keeping it available to those entitled to it.

Key points

  • Cybersecurity protects confidentiality, integrity and availability.
  • It spans technology, process and people, not just software.
  • Most successful breaches begin with a person, not a technical flaw.
  • Defence in depth: several independent layers, so one failure is not fatal.
  • Security is a continuing process, not a product you install once.
  • Perfect security does not exist; the goal is managed, acceptable risk.

Example

A bank can have firewalls, encryption and monitoring, and still lose funds because one employee approved a fraudulent transfer after a convincing phone call. The technology worked exactly as designed.

Why this matters

Everything in this course — networking, Linux, SOC work, forensics, AI defences — serves these three goals. Keeping them in mind is what turns a list of tools into a coherent practice.

questions.explanation: Social engineering and human error are involved in the large majority of successful attacks.

lessons.title: 1.3 Why AI and Cybersecurity Matter
lessons.html:
📖 Why AI and Cybersecurity Matter
Attack volume outgrew human capacity; defence had to change shape.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Why AI and Cybersecurity Matter

Why AI and Cybersecurity Matter is the focus of this Introduction to AI and Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to explain how AI and cybersecurity protect people, data, and systems.

artificial intelligence

Computer systems designed to perform tasks associated with human intelligence.

cybersecurity

Protection of systems, networks, and data from digital threats.

threat

A circumstance or actor capable of causing harm.

A medium-sized organisation can generate millions of security events a day. No team can read them. AI is used to reduce that flood to the small number of events a human should actually look at.

The same technology is available to attackers. AI writes more convincing phishing, generates malware variants faster, and automates reconnaissance. This is why the two subjects are now taught together rather than separately.

Key points

  • Event volume long ago exceeded what human analysts can review.
  • AI triages: it reduces millions of events to a reviewable handful.
  • Attackers use the same tools, so defensive AI is not optional.
  • AI reduces alert fatigue, a leading cause of missed incidents.
  • AI is a force multiplier for analysts, not a replacement for them.
  • Every AI defence introduces new attack surface of its own.

Example

A SOC receives 4 million events overnight. Rules reduce that to 20,000 alerts, still unreadable. A model ranks them and surfaces 40 for review, of which three are genuine. Without that step the three would have been missed.

Why this matters

This is the argument for the whole course. Understanding both sides — what AI gives defenders and what it gives attackers — is what the job now requires.

questions.explanation: The same capabilities that help defenders also make attacks faster, cheaper and more convincing.

lessons.title: 1.4 Types of Cyber Threats
lessons.html:
📖 Types of Cyber Threats
A small number of threat families account for most real incidents.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Types of Cyber Threats

Types of Cyber Threats is the focus of this Introduction to AI and Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to explain how AI and cybersecurity protect people, data, and systems.

artificial intelligence

Computer systems designed to perform tasks associated with human intelligence.

cybersecurity

Protection of systems, networks, and data from digital threats.

threat

A circumstance or actor capable of causing harm.

Threats are usually grouped by method: malware (malicious software), social engineering (manipulating people), network attacks, application attacks, and insider threats.

Ransomware — encrypting an organisation's data and demanding payment — combines several of these, and is currently the most financially damaging category for most organisations.

Key points

  • Malware: viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, ransomware.
  • Phishing: fraudulent messages that harvest credentials or deliver malware.
  • Ransomware: encrypts data and demands payment for its return.
  • Denial of service: overwhelms a service so legitimate users cannot reach it.
  • Insider threat: harm caused by someone with legitimate access.
  • Supply chain: compromising a trusted supplier to reach their customers.

Example

A ransomware incident typically starts with a phishing email, escalates through stolen credentials, spreads across the network, and only then encrypts files. Each stage was an opportunity to detect it.

Why this matters

Knowing the families tells you what to look for. Detection, forensics and incident response in later modules are all organised around these categories.

lessons.title: 1.5 Cybersecurity Roles and Careers
lessons.html:
📖 Cybersecurity Roles and Careers
The field is wider than 'hacker' — and most of it is defensive.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Cybersecurity Roles and Careers

Cybersecurity Roles and Careers is the focus of this Introduction to AI and Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to explain how AI and cybersecurity protect people, data, and systems.

artificial intelligence

Computer systems designed to perform tasks associated with human intelligence.

cybersecurity

Protection of systems, networks, and data from digital threats.

threat

A circumstance or actor capable of causing harm.

Security work divides broadly into blue team (defence: SOC analysts, incident responders, forensics), red team (authorised offensive testing: penetration testers), and governance (risk, compliance, policy, audit).

Most entry-level roles are blue team, usually SOC Analyst Tier 1: monitoring alerts, triaging them, and escalating what matters. That is the role this course prepares you for.

Key points

  • SOC Analyst — monitors and triages alerts; the common entry point.
  • Incident Responder — contains and remediates confirmed incidents.
  • Digital Forensics Analyst — investigates what happened, preserving evidence.
  • Penetration Tester — tests defences under written authorisation.
  • Security Engineer — builds and maintains defensive systems.
  • GRC Analyst — governance, risk and compliance; no coding required.

Example

A common path: help desk → SOC Analyst Tier 1 → Tier 2 → incident response or threat hunting. Employers value demonstrable log-reading and clear incident write-ups over certifications alone.

Why this matters

Knowing the roles helps you aim your study. Remote SOC work is genuinely accessible from Liberia, and the skills in Modules 9 to 11 are exactly what those roles interview on.

lessons.title: 1.6 How AI Is Used in Cybersecurity
lessons.html:
📖 How AI Is Used in Cybersecurity
Six practical uses, all of them about reducing what a human has to read.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

How AI Is Used in Cybersecurity

How AI Is Used in Cybersecurity is the focus of this Introduction to AI and Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to explain how AI and cybersecurity protect people, data, and systems.

artificial intelligence

Computer systems designed to perform tasks associated with human intelligence.

cybersecurity

Protection of systems, networks, and data from digital threats.

threat

A circumstance or actor capable of causing harm.

AI appears in security products for detection, triage, phishing analysis, malware classification, log summarisation and automation. In every case the goal is the same: turn an unmanageable volume into a manageable one.

It is not magic. Models produce false positives and false negatives, they degrade as attacker behaviour shifts, and they can be deliberately manipulated. Those limitations are covered in Module 8 and attacked directly in Module 12.

Key points

  • Anomaly detection: flagging behaviour unlike the established baseline.
  • Alert triage: ranking alerts so analysts see the important ones first.
  • Phishing analysis: scoring messages on many signals at once.
  • Malware classification: grouping unknown files by similarity to known families.
  • Log summarisation: turning thousands of lines into a readable account.
  • Automation: drafting queries, enrichment and first-draft reports.

Example

An analyst pastes 400 lines of authentication logs into an assistant and asks what is unusual. It highlights one account authenticating from two countries eleven minutes apart. The analyst verifies it directly — the tool found it, the human confirmed it.

Why this matters

This is the pattern the rest of the course teaches: AI narrows the field, the analyst decides. Reversing that order is how AI-assisted security goes wrong.

lessons.title: 2.1 Computer Hardware and Software
lessons.html:
📖 Computer Hardware and Software
You cannot secure a machine whose parts you cannot name.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Computer Hardware and Software

Computer Hardware and Software is the focus of this Computer and Networking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand computers, networks, addressing, and internet communication.

network

Connected devices that exchange data and share resources.

protocol

A defined set of rules for communication between systems.

packet

A formatted unit of data transmitted across a network.

Hardware is the physical machine: CPU, RAM, storage, network interface. Software is what runs on it: firmware, the operating system, and applications. Security incidents touch every layer.

The layer matters for defence. Malware in an application is removable; malware in firmware survives reinstalling the operating system, which is why firmware compromise is treated so seriously.

Key points

  • CPU executes instructions; RAM holds running data and is lost on power-off.
  • Storage (HDD/SSD) persists data; forensics recovers from it.
  • Firmware (BIOS/UEFI) runs before the operating system starts.
  • Operating system manages hardware and enforces access control.
  • RAM is volatile — capture it before shutting a suspect machine down.
  • Compromise low in the stack is harder to detect and harder to remove.

Example

A responder who powers off a compromised laptop to “stop the attack” destroys the RAM contents — running processes, network connections, sometimes encryption keys. The evidence that would have explained the incident is gone.

Why this matters

Forensics in Module 11 depends entirely on knowing which layer holds which evidence and which of it disappears when the power does.

lessons.title: 2.2 Operating Systems
lessons.html:
📖 Operating Systems
The operating system is where most security controls actually live.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Operating Systems

Operating Systems is the focus of this Computer and Networking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand computers, networks, addressing, and internet communication.

network

Connected devices that exchange data and share resources.

protocol

A defined set of rules for communication between systems.

packet

A formatted unit of data transmitted across a network.

An operating system manages hardware, runs processes, and — critically for security — decides who may do what. Windows, Linux and macOS all implement user accounts, file permissions and privilege separation, differently but for the same purpose.

The core idea is privilege separation: ordinary users cannot alter the system, and only administrative accounts can. Most attacks therefore aim at gaining administrative privilege.

Key points

  • The OS enforces user accounts, file permissions and process isolation.
  • Privilege escalation is an attacker moving from user to administrator.
  • Windows uses Administrator; Linux uses root and sudo.
  • Run daily work as an unprivileged user — the single cheapest control there is.
  • Patching the OS closes the flaws privilege escalation relies on.
  • System logs are produced by the OS and are the analyst's primary evidence.

Example

Ransomware that runs as an ordinary user can encrypt that user's documents. The same ransomware running as administrator can encrypt the whole machine, disable backups and clear the logs. The account it landed in decided the scale of the incident.

Why this matters

Modules 4 and 10 build on this: Linux permissions, and the log data the operating system produces for a SOC to read.

lessons.title: 2.3 Files, Processes, and Services
lessons.html:
📖 Files, Processes, and Services
Three things to look at on any machine you suspect.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Files, Processes, and Services

Files, Processes, and Services is the focus of this Computer and Networking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand computers, networks, addressing, and internet communication.

network

Connected devices that exchange data and share resources.

protocol

A defined set of rules for communication between systems.

packet

A formatted unit of data transmitted across a network.

A file is data at rest. A process is a running program. A service is a process that starts automatically and keeps running in the background.

Attackers use all three: a malicious file on disk, a process running in memory, and a service to survive reboots. Establishing persistence — surviving a restart — almost always involves a service or a scheduled task.

Key points

  • Files are at rest; processes are running; services run automatically.
  • Persistence means surviving reboot, usually via a service or scheduled task.
  • A process has a PID, a parent, an owning user and a command line.
  • Suspicious signs: an odd parent process, an unusual path, a random-looking name.
  • Some malware runs only in memory, leaving no file to find.
  • Windows: Task Manager and services.msc. Linux: ps, top and systemctl.

Example

An investigation finds a process named svch0st.exe — a zero for the letter o — running from a user's Downloads folder rather than the system directory, with a browser as its parent. Three anomalies, each visible in a process listing.

Why this matters

Alert triage in Module 10 and malware response in Module 11 both begin exactly here: what is running, where did it come from, and what started it.

lessons.title: 2.4 What Is a Computer Network?
lessons.html:
📖 What Is a Computer Network?
Machines that can reach one another — which is exactly what an attacker wants.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

What Is a Computer Network?

What Is a Computer Network? is the focus of this Computer and Networking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand computers, networks, addressing, and internet communication.

network

Connected devices that exchange data and share resources.

protocol

A defined set of rules for communication between systems.

packet

A formatted unit of data transmitted across a network.

A network connects devices so they can exchange data. A LAN covers one site; a WAN connects sites; the internet connects networks globally.

Connectivity is the attack surface. Once inside a flat network, an attacker can reach every machine on it. Segmentation — dividing the network so compromise of one part does not expose the rest — is a core defensive control.

Key points

  • A LAN is local; a WAN spans sites; the internet joins networks.
  • A switch connects devices; a router connects networks.
  • Lateral movement is an attacker spreading from one machine to others.
  • Segmentation limits how far a compromise can reach.
  • A flat network means one compromised machine can reach everything.
  • Network diagrams and asset inventories are security documents, not just IT ones.

Example

Ransomware lands on a receptionist's PC. On a flat network it reaches the file server and the backups within minutes. On a segmented network it reaches only the office subnet, and the servers survive.

Why this matters

Segmentation is one of the few controls that changes an incident's scale rather than its likelihood, which is why network design belongs in a security course.

lessons.title: 2.5 IP Addresses
lessons.html:
📖 IP Addresses
The address that identifies a device on a network — and the first thing you check in a log.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

IP Addresses

IP Addresses is the focus of this Computer and Networking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand computers, networks, addressing, and internet communication.

network

Connected devices that exchange data and share resources.

protocol

A defined set of rules for communication between systems.

packet

A formatted unit of data transmitted across a network.

An IP address identifies a device so traffic can reach it. IPv4 uses four numbers (192.168.1.10); IPv6 uses a longer hexadecimal form. Addresses are either private (inside a network) or public (reachable from the internet).

For an analyst, the IP address is the starting point of almost every investigation: which machine, whose account, which country, and is that expected?

Key points

  • Private ranges: 10.x.x.x, 172.16–31.x.x, 192.168.x.x — not routable on the internet.
  • Public addresses are internet-reachable and are what external logs record.
  • NAT lets many private addresses share one public address.
  • Static addresses stay fixed; dynamic ones are assigned by DHCP.
  • Geolocation of an IP is approximate and easily disguised by VPN or proxy.
  • An IP alone does not identify a person — correlate it with account and device.

Example

A login is recorded from a public address geolocating to another continent, eleven minutes after a login from the office. The distance is impossible — an impossible travel alert, and one of the most reliable signals in identity monitoring.

Why this matters

Reading logs in Modules 9 to 11 depends on this. Knowing which addresses are internal and which are not is what separates ordinary traffic from something worth investigating.

lessons.title: 2.6 MAC Addresses
lessons.html:
📖 MAC Addresses
A hardware address that identifies a device on the local network segment.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

MAC Addresses

MAC Addresses is the focus of this Computer and Networking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand computers, networks, addressing, and internet communication.

network

Connected devices that exchange data and share resources.

protocol

A defined set of rules for communication between systems.

packet

A formatted unit of data transmitted across a network.

A MAC address is a 48-bit identifier burned into a network interface, written as six hexadecimal pairs such as 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. It operates at the link layer, so it is used only within a local network segment.

Unlike an IP address, a MAC address does not travel across routers. That makes it useful for identifying a physical device inside a network, and useless for tracing anything beyond it.

Key points

  • 48 bits, written as six hexadecimal pairs.
  • Used within a local segment only — routers do not forward it.
  • The first three pairs identify the manufacturer (the OUI).
  • MAC addresses can be spoofed in software, so they are weak as an access control.
  • MAC filtering on Wi-Fi is a deterrent, not a security control.
  • DHCP and switch tables map MAC addresses to IP addresses and ports.

Example

An investigation traces a rogue device by its MAC address to a specific switch port in a meeting room. The OUI shows the manufacturer, which does not match any issued asset — strong evidence of an unauthorised device.

Why this matters

Asset identification during an incident often comes down to a MAC address, because it survives the DHCP lease changes that make IP addresses unreliable over time.

questions.explanation: MAC addresses are link-layer identifiers and are not forwarded across routers.

questions.question: Why is MAC filtering a weak security control?
options: MAC addresses can be spoofed in software
questions.explanation: Because a MAC address can be changed by software, filtering on it deters rather than prevents.

questions.question: What do the first three pairs of a MAC address indicate?
questions.explanation: The organisationally unique identifier identifies the interface manufacturer.

lessons.title: 2.7 DNS and DHCP
lessons.html:
📖 DNS and DHCP
One turns names into addresses; the other hands addresses out. Both are attacker targets.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

DNS and DHCP

DNS and DHCP is the focus of this Computer and Networking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand computers, networks, addressing, and internet communication.

network

Connected devices that exchange data and share resources.

protocol

A defined set of rules for communication between systems.

packet

A formatted unit of data transmitted across a network.

DNS resolves human-readable names into IP addresses. DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses to devices joining a network.

DNS logs are among the most valuable data a defender has, because almost every action starts with a name lookup — including malware contacting its command and control server.

Key points

  • DNS: name → IP address. DHCP: assigns addresses automatically.
  • DNS logs reveal what a machine tried to contact, even when the connection failed.
  • DNS tunnelling hides stolen data inside DNS queries.
  • Newly registered or algorithmically generated domains are a common malware signal.
  • DHCP logs map an IP address to a device at a point in time — essential for attribution.
  • Because DHCP leases change, always record the time alongside an IP address.

Example

A workstation resolves a 40-character random domain registered two days earlier, several times an hour. No data left the network because the firewall blocked it — but the DNS log alone identified the infection.

Why this matters

DNS is the single richest log source for detection, and DHCP is what lets you say which physical machine an address belonged to at the time of an incident.

questions.question: What does DNS do?
options: Resolves domain names into IP addresses
questions.explanation: DNS translates human-readable names into the IP addresses machines use.

questions.question: Why are DNS logs valuable to defenders?
options: They show what a machine tried to contact, even when blocked
questions.explanation: The lookup happens before the connection, so DNS records attempts that never succeeded.

questions.question: Why must a time be recorded alongside an IP address?
options: It is a legal requirement only
DHCP leases change, so the same address maps to different devices over time
questions.explanation: Without a timestamp an IP address cannot be tied to a specific device, because leases are reassigned.

lessons.title: 2.8 Ports and Protocols
lessons.html:
📖 Ports and Protocols
The port number tells you what a connection was for.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Ports and Protocols

Ports and Protocols is the focus of this Computer and Networking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand computers, networks, addressing, and internet communication.

network

Connected devices that exchange data and share resources.

protocol

A defined set of rules for communication between systems.

packet

A formatted unit of data transmitted across a network.

An IP address identifies a machine; a port identifies the service on it. A protocol defines the rules of the conversation. Together they tell an analyst what a connection was doing.

Knowing the common ports lets you read a firewall log at a glance, and lets you spot the anomalies: a service on an unexpected port, or plain-text protocols where encrypted ones should be.

Key points

  • 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 22 SSH, 53 DNS, 25 SMTP.
  • 3389 RDP and 445 SMB are heavily targeted — never expose them to the internet.
  • TCP is connection-oriented and reliable; UDP is fast and connectionless.
  • Plain-text protocols (FTP, Telnet, HTTP) expose credentials in transit.
  • A service listening on an unusual high port deserves investigation.
  • Closing unused ports reduces attack surface at no cost.

Example

A firewall log shows outbound traffic on port 4444 from an internal workstation to an external address. No legitimate business service uses it. The port number alone was enough to escalate.

Why this matters

Port knowledge underpins network scanning in Module 5 and alert triage in Module 10 — most network alerts are ultimately a judgement about whether a port and destination make sense together.

questions.question: Which port does HTTPS use by default?
questions.explanation: HTTPS uses TCP port 443, while unencrypted HTTP uses port 80.

questions.question: Why should RDP (port 3389) never be exposed directly to the internet?
options: It is heavily targeted for brute-force and exploitation
questions.explanation: Internet-exposed RDP is one of the most common initial access routes for ransomware.

questions.question: What is the main risk of plain-text protocols such as Telnet and FTP?
options: Credentials and data are exposed in transit
questions.explanation: Without encryption, anyone able to observe the traffic can read the credentials.

lessons.title: 2.9 TCP/IP Fundamentals
lessons.html:
📖 TCP/IP Fundamentals
The layered model that explains where each security control sits.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

TCP/IP Fundamentals

TCP/IP Fundamentals is the focus of this Computer and Networking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand computers, networks, addressing, and internet communication.

network

Connected devices that exchange data and share resources.

protocol

A defined set of rules for communication between systems.

packet

A formatted unit of data transmitted across a network.

TCP/IP organises networking into layers: link, internet, transport and application. Each layer has its own job, and each has its own attacks and its own defences.

TCP establishes a connection with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) and guarantees delivery. UDP does neither, which makes it fast and makes it easy to forge.

Key points

  • Layers: link, internet (IP), transport (TCP/UDP), application (HTTP, DNS).
  • TCP handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK.
  • Half-open connections in bulk indicate a SYN flood or a stealth scan.
  • UDP is connectionless, so its source address is trivially spoofed.
  • Firewalls work mainly at the transport layer; WAFs at the application layer.
  • Encryption at one layer does not protect the layers below it.

Example

A server logs thousands of SYN packets with no completing ACK. Each half-open connection consumes a slot in the connection table; enough of them and legitimate users cannot connect. That is a SYN flood, and it is visible in the handshake pattern.

Why this matters

The layer model is how you decide which control applies to which problem — and why a firewall cannot stop an SQL injection carried inside legitimate HTTPS traffic.

questions.question: What are the three steps of the TCP handshake?
questions.explanation: A TCP connection is established with SYN, SYN-ACK and then ACK.

questions.question: Why is UDP easier to spoof than TCP?
options: It is connectionless, so no handshake proves the source
questions.explanation: Without a handshake there is nothing to confirm the sender's address is genuine.

questions.question: Why can a network firewall miss an SQL injection attack?
options: The attack rides inside legitimate application-layer traffic
questions.explanation: Transport-layer filtering sees an allowed HTTPS connection; the attack is in the application content.

lessons.title: 2.10 How the Internet Works
lessons.html:
📖 How the Internet Works
Following one request end to end explains most of network security.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

How the Internet Works

How the Internet Works is the focus of this Computer and Networking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand computers, networks, addressing, and internet communication.

network

Connected devices that exchange data and share resources.

protocol

A defined set of rules for communication between systems.

packet

A formatted unit of data transmitted across a network.

Opening a web page involves DNS resolution, a TCP connection, a TLS handshake, and then the HTTP request itself. Each step is a place where something can be observed, blocked, or attacked.

Routing means the request crosses networks you do not control. That is the reason encryption in transit is not optional — you must assume the path is hostile.

Key points

  • Steps: DNS lookup → TCP connection → TLS handshake → HTTP request.
  • Traffic crosses networks you neither own nor trust.
  • TLS encrypts content in transit; it does not vouch for the site's honesty.
  • A valid certificate proves the name, not that the operator is trustworthy.
  • Proxies and VPNs change the apparent source of a request.
  • Each step produces a log an analyst can correlate.

Example

A single page visit leaves a DNS log, a firewall connection log, a proxy log and a web server log. Correlating those four is how an analyst reconstructs what a user actually did — and each records a different part of it.

Why this matters

This end-to-end picture is the foundation for web security in Module 6 and for the log correlation that all SOC work depends on.

questions.question: What is the first step when a browser opens a website by name?
options: A DNS lookup to resolve the name
questions.explanation: The name must be resolved to an IP address before any connection can be made.

questions.question: What does a valid TLS certificate prove?
options: The connection is to the named domain and is encrypted
questions.explanation: TLS authenticates the domain name and encrypts the channel; it says nothing about the operator's intent.

questions.question: Why is encryption in transit necessary?
options: Traffic crosses networks you do not control
questions.explanation: Because the path is untrusted, content must be protected independently of the network carrying it.

lessons.title: 3.1 CIA Triad: Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability
lessons.html:
📖 CIA Triad: Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability
Three words that classify every security control and every incident.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

CIA Triad: Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability

CIA Triad: Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability is the focus of this Cybersecurity Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to apply foundational controls that protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

asset

Data, hardware, software, or services requiring protection.

security control

A safeguard that reduces risk.

risk

The combination of threat likelihood and potential impact.

Confidentiality keeps data from those not entitled to it. Integrity keeps it accurate and unaltered. Availability keeps it reachable when needed.

Every incident damages at least one of the three, and every control protects at least one. Naming which is affected is the first step in classifying an incident and choosing a response.

Key points

  • Confidentiality — encryption, access control, classification.
  • Integrity — hashing, digital signatures, change control, audit logs.
  • Availability — backups, redundancy, DDoS protection, capacity.
  • The three often conflict; strengthening one can weaken another.
  • Ransomware attacks availability and, with data theft, confidentiality too.
  • Classify an incident by which of the three it damaged.

Example

A data breach damages confidentiality. A tampered financial record damages integrity. A DDoS attack damages availability. Ransomware with data theft damages all three — which is why it is the costliest category.

Why this matters

The triad is the vocabulary of the whole profession. Risk assessments, incident reports and audit findings are all written in these terms.

lessons.html: Quick check: review the notes and complete the two practice steps, then answer these to confirm you understood CIA Triad: Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability.

questions.question: A denial-of-service attack primarily damages which property?
questions.explanation: A DDoS prevents legitimate users from reaching a service, which is an availability failure.

questions.question: Which control most directly protects integrity?
questions.explanation: Hashes and signatures detect whether data has been altered, which is what integrity means.

questions.question: Why can strengthening one CIA property weaken another?
options: Controls trade off, such as strict access reducing availability
questions.explanation: Tighter confidentiality controls often make legitimate access slower or harder, reducing availability.

lessons.title: 3.2 Authentication and Authorization
lessons.html:
📖 Authentication and Authorization
One asks who you are; the other asks what you may do.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Authentication and Authorization

Authentication and Authorization is the focus of this Cybersecurity Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to apply foundational controls that protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

asset

Data, hardware, software, or services requiring protection.

security control

A safeguard that reduces risk.

risk

The combination of threat likelihood and potential impact.

Authentication proves identity — a password, a token, a fingerprint. Authorization decides what that proven identity is permitted to do.

They fail differently. Weak authentication lets the wrong person in. Weak authorization lets the right person do the wrong thing, which is why over-privileged accounts are so damaging when compromised.

Key points

  • Authentication = who you are. Authorization = what you may do.
  • Factors: something you know, something you have, something you are.
  • Least privilege: grant only the access the role actually requires.
  • Accounting completes the picture — log what was done.
  • Authorization must be enforced server-side; client-side checks are advisory only.
  • Review and remove access when people change roles or leave.

Example

A finance clerk authenticates correctly and then opens HR salary records. Authentication worked; authorization did not. The account had accumulated permissions from a previous role that nobody removed.

Why this matters

Access control failures are among the most common findings in real assessments, and they are what Module 6's access control lesson and Module 13's cloud IAM lesson build on.

lessons.html: Quick check: review the notes and complete the two practice steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Authentication and Authorization.

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication proves identity; authorization decides permitted actions
questions.explanation: Identity is established first, then permissions are evaluated for that identity.

questions.question: What does the principle of least privilege require?
options: Grant only the access a role genuinely requires
Access is reviewed once a decade
questions.explanation: Limiting permissions limits the damage when an account is compromised or misused.

questions.question: Why must authorization checks run server-side?
options: Client-side checks can be bypassed by the user
questions.explanation: Anything enforced only in the browser can be modified or skipped by an attacker.

lessons.title: 3.3 Password Security
lessons.html:
📖 Password Security
Length beats complexity, and reuse is the real problem.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Password Security

Password Security is the focus of this Cybersecurity Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to apply foundational controls that protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

asset

Data, hardware, software, or services requiring protection.

security control

A safeguard that reduces risk.

risk

The combination of threat likelihood and potential impact.

Password strength comes mainly from length and unpredictability. A long passphrase resists guessing far better than a short string of substituted characters, which attackers' tools expect.

The bigger risk is reuse. When one site is breached, attackers replay those credentials everywhere else — an attack called credential stuffing, and it needs no technical skill at all.

Key points

  • Length matters more than symbol substitution; passphrases are strong and memorable.
  • Never reuse passwords across services.
  • Credential stuffing replays breached credentials against other sites.
  • Password managers make unique passwords practical.
  • Systems store password hashes, never the passwords themselves.
  • Forced frequent rotation encourages weak, predictable variations.

Example

P@ssw0rd! looks complex and appears in every cracking dictionary. correct-battery-village-lantern is longer, easier to remember, and vastly harder to guess.

Why this matters

Compromised credentials remain the leading initial access method in real breaches, which makes this the highest-impact user-facing control in the course.

lessons.html: Quick check: review the notes and complete the two practice steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Password Security.

questions.question: What contributes most to password strength?
questions.explanation: Long, unpredictable passphrases resist guessing far better than short substituted strings.

questions.question: What is credential stuffing?
options: Replaying credentials from one breach against other services
questions.explanation: Because people reuse passwords, credentials stolen from one site often work elsewhere.

questions.question: How should a system store user passwords?
questions.explanation: Hashing with a salt means the original password cannot be recovered from a stolen database.

lessons.title: 3.4 Multi-Factor Authentication
lessons.html:
📖 Multi-Factor Authentication
The single most effective control against stolen credentials.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Multi-Factor Authentication

Multi-Factor Authentication is the focus of this Cybersecurity Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to apply foundational controls that protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

asset

Data, hardware, software, or services requiring protection.

security control

A safeguard that reduces risk.

risk

The combination of threat likelihood and potential impact.

MFA requires evidence from more than one category: something you know, something you have, something you are. A stolen password alone then becomes insufficient.

Not all factors are equal. SMS codes can be intercepted through SIM swapping; authenticator apps are stronger; hardware security keys resist phishing entirely because they verify the site's identity as well as yours.

Key points

  • Factors: something you know, have, or are — two different categories.
  • Two passwords are not MFA; both are the same factor.
  • Strength order: SMS < authenticator app < hardware security key.
  • SMS is vulnerable to SIM swapping.
  • MFA fatigue: repeated push prompts until a tired user approves one.
  • Hardware keys resist phishing because they check the site's domain.

Example

An attacker with a valid password triggers push notifications at 2am until the user taps approve to stop them. That is MFA fatigue — and it is why number-matching prompts replaced simple approve buttons.

Why this matters

MFA blocks the overwhelming majority of credential-based attacks. Knowing which implementations are weak is what stops it becoming a false sense of security.

lessons.html: Quick check: review the notes and complete the two practice steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Multi-Factor Authentication.

questions.question: Which combination is genuine multi-factor authentication?
options: A password and a code from an authenticator app
A password and a security question
questions.explanation: MFA requires factors from different categories; a password and a device-generated code qualify.

questions.question: Why is SMS the weakest common MFA factor?
options: It is vulnerable to SIM swapping and interception
questions.explanation: An attacker who takes over the phone number receives the codes.

questions.question: What is MFA fatigue?
options: Flooding a user with push prompts until one is approved
questions.explanation: Repeated prompts wear the user down until they approve one to stop the notifications.

lessons.title: 3.5 Encryption Basics
lessons.html:
📖 Encryption Basics
Scrambling data so that only a key holder can read it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Encryption Basics

Encryption Basics is the focus of this Cybersecurity Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to apply foundational controls that protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

asset

Data, hardware, software, or services requiring protection.

security control

A safeguard that reduces risk.

risk

The combination of threat likelihood and potential impact.

Symmetric encryption uses one key for both directions and is fast — AES is the standard. Asymmetric encryption uses a public/private key pair and solves the problem of exchanging keys safely.

Hashing is not encryption. A hash is one-way and cannot be reversed; it proves that data has not changed. Encryption protects confidentiality; hashing protects integrity.

Key points

  • Symmetric (AES): one shared key, fast, used for bulk data.
  • Asymmetric (RSA, ECC): key pair, solves key exchange, slower.
  • Hashing (SHA-256) is one-way and verifies integrity, not confidentiality.
  • TLS uses asymmetric to agree a key, then symmetric for the traffic.
  • Encryption at rest protects stored data; in transit protects moving data.
  • The security lies in the key, never in keeping the algorithm secret.

Example

TLS begins with an asymmetric handshake to agree a shared secret, then switches to fast symmetric encryption for the actual data. Each algorithm is used for what it does best.

Why this matters

Encryption underpins the web security, cloud data protection and forensics work later in the course, and the encryption/hashing distinction is tested constantly in interviews.

questions.question: What is the key difference between hashing and encryption?
options: Hashing is one-way and cannot be reversed
questions.explanation: Encryption is reversible with a key; hashing is a one-way function used to verify integrity.

questions.question: Why does TLS use both asymmetric and symmetric encryption?
options: Asymmetric safely agrees a key; symmetric then encrypts data quickly
questions.explanation: Each is used for its strength: key exchange without a shared secret, then fast bulk encryption.

questions.question: Where does the security of a modern cipher lie?
options: In the secrecy of the key
questions.explanation: Algorithms are public and reviewed; only the key must remain secret.

lessons.title: 3.6 Firewalls
lessons.html:
📖 Firewalls
A policy enforcement point that decides which traffic is allowed through.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Firewalls

Firewalls is the focus of this Cybersecurity Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to apply foundational controls that protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

asset

Data, hardware, software, or services requiring protection.

security control

A safeguard that reduces risk.

risk

The combination of threat likelihood and potential impact.

A firewall inspects traffic and permits or blocks it against a ruleset. Network firewalls sit at boundaries; host firewalls run on individual machines; next-generation firewalls also inspect applications and users.

The strongest configuration is default deny: block everything, then permit only what is required. The opposite — permitting everything except known-bad — fails against anything new.

Key points

  • Default deny is the correct posture; allow only what is needed.
  • Rules are evaluated in order, so rule order changes behaviour.
  • Egress (outbound) filtering matters as much as ingress — it blocks exfiltration.
  • A firewall cannot inspect encrypted content unless it terminates TLS.
  • Host firewalls limit lateral movement inside the network.
  • Firewall logs are a primary detection source; deny events are as useful as allows.

Example

Malware on a workstation tries to reach its command server on an unusual port. Ingress rules were irrelevant — the connection was outbound. Only egress filtering stopped it, and the deny log raised the alert.

Why this matters

Most organisations filter inbound traffic carefully and outbound traffic barely at all, which is precisely the gap data exfiltration uses.

questions.question: What does a 'default deny' firewall policy mean?
options: Block everything, then permit only what is required
questions.explanation: Default deny fails safe: anything not explicitly permitted, including novel traffic, is blocked.

questions.question: Why does egress filtering matter?
options: It blocks outbound connections used for exfiltration and command and control
questions.explanation: Outbound filtering catches compromised hosts calling out, which inbound rules never see.

questions.question: Why can a firewall miss threats inside encrypted traffic?
options: It cannot read the content unless it terminates TLS
questions.explanation: Without TLS inspection the firewall sees only the connection, not what it carries.

lessons.title: 3.7 Antivirus and Endpoint Security
lessons.html:
📖 Antivirus and Endpoint Security
Signatures catch the known; behaviour catches the rest.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Antivirus and Endpoint Security

Antivirus and Endpoint Security is the focus of this Cybersecurity Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to apply foundational controls that protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

asset

Data, hardware, software, or services requiring protection.

security control

A safeguard that reduces risk.

risk

The combination of threat likelihood and potential impact.

Traditional antivirus matches files against signatures of known malware. That works only for threats already catalogued, which is why modern EDR (endpoint detection and response) adds behavioural monitoring.

EDR watches what a process does — spawning shells, encrypting files rapidly, contacting unusual addresses — and can isolate a machine from the network automatically.

Key points

  • Signature detection catches known malware only.
  • Behavioural detection catches novel and fileless attacks.
  • EDR records endpoint activity, enabling investigation after the fact.
  • Fileless malware lives in memory and leaves no file to scan.
  • EDR can isolate a host from the network as an automated containment step.
  • Endpoint agents produce the telemetry a SOC investigates.

Example

A document opens PowerShell, which downloads and runs code entirely in memory. No file is written, so signature scanning finds nothing. The behaviour — an office document spawning a scripting engine — is what triggers the alert.

Why this matters

Endpoint telemetry is the evidence base for SOC triage in Module 10 and for the malware response process in Module 11.

questions.question: What is the main limitation of signature-based antivirus?
options: It detects only malware that has already been catalogued
questions.explanation: Signatures match known samples, so novel or modified malware passes undetected.

questions.question: Why does fileless malware evade traditional antivirus?
options: It runs in memory and writes no file to scan
questions.explanation: Signature scanning inspects files, and fileless attacks never create one.

questions.question: What additional capability does EDR provide over antivirus?
options: Behavioural monitoring, recorded telemetry and host isolation
questions.explanation: EDR watches process behaviour, retains activity history for investigation, and can contain a host.

lessons.title: 3.8 Security Policies
lessons.html:
📖 Security Policies
Written rules that make expected behaviour enforceable.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Security Policies

Security Policies is the focus of this Cybersecurity Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to apply foundational controls that protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

asset

Data, hardware, software, or services requiring protection.

security control

A safeguard that reduces risk.

risk

The combination of threat likelihood and potential impact.

A security policy states what is required, who is responsible, and what happens when it is not followed. Without one, controls are opinions and breaches of them cannot be acted upon.

Policies must be specific, achievable and enforced. A policy nobody can follow gets ignored, and an ignored policy is worse than none because it creates false assurance in an audit.

Key points

  • A policy states requirements; a procedure states the steps to meet them.
  • Common policies: acceptable use, access control, password, incident response, data classification.
  • Policies must be approved by management to carry authority.
  • They require review on a schedule, not just at creation.
  • An unenforceable policy creates false assurance rather than protection.
  • Staff must be told what the policy says — publication is part of enforcement.

Example

A policy requiring 30-character passwords with monthly rotation produces sticky notes on monitors. The written control looks strong in an audit and has actively reduced security in practice.

Why this matters

Governance work is a real and accessible career path, and policy is what turns the technical controls in this course into an organisational programme.

questions.question: What is the difference between a policy and a procedure?
options: A policy states requirements; a procedure states the steps
A procedure is approved by management
questions.explanation: Policies define what must be achieved; procedures describe how to achieve it.

questions.question: Why is an unenforceable policy worse than none?
options: It creates false assurance while being ignored in practice
questions.explanation: An ignored policy looks like a control during audit while providing no actual protection.

questions.question: What makes a security policy authoritative?
options: Management approval and publication to staff
questions.explanation: Without management endorsement and communication, a policy cannot be enforced.

lessons.title: 3.9 Risk Management
lessons.html:
📖 Risk Management
Security decisions are risk decisions, and risk is likelihood times impact.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Risk Management

Risk Management is the focus of this Cybersecurity Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to apply foundational controls that protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

asset

Data, hardware, software, or services requiring protection.

security control

A safeguard that reduces risk.

risk

The combination of threat likelihood and potential impact.

Risk management identifies what could go wrong, how likely it is, and how bad it would be. Controls are then chosen where they reduce the most risk for the cost — not where they are most interesting.

The four responses are mitigate (reduce it), transfer (insure or outsource it), avoid (stop the activity) and accept (document and live with it).

Key points

  • Risk = likelihood × impact.
  • Responses: mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept.
  • Accepting a risk is legitimate — if it is documented and approved.
  • A vulnerability is a weakness; a threat is what might exploit it.
  • Residual risk is what remains after controls are applied.
  • Prioritise by risk reduced per unit of cost, not by technical interest.

Example

A rarely used legacy server has a serious vulnerability but holds no sensitive data and is unreachable from the internet. High vulnerability, low risk. Patching the internet-facing payroll system first is the correct call.

Why this matters

Risk language is how security is justified to people who control budgets, and it is what separates a security professional from a technician.

lessons.html: Quick check: review the notes and complete the two practice steps, then answer these to confirm you understood Risk Management.

questions.explanation: Risk combines how likely an event is with how damaging it would be.

questions.question: Which is a legitimate response to an identified risk?
options: Formally accepting it with documentation and approval
questions.explanation: Accepting risk is valid when it is consciously decided, documented and approved.

questions.question: What is residual risk?
options: Risk remaining after controls are applied
questions.explanation: Controls reduce but rarely eliminate risk; what remains is residual risk.

lessons.title: 3.10 Security Awareness
lessons.html:
📖 Security Awareness
Training the people attackers actually target.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Security Awareness

Security Awareness is the focus of this Cybersecurity Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to apply foundational controls that protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

asset

Data, hardware, software, or services requiring protection.

security control

A safeguard that reduces risk.

risk

The combination of threat likelihood and potential impact.

The majority of successful breaches involve a person doing something reasonable-looking. Awareness training aims to make that moment recognisable: an unexpected urgent request, an unfamiliar sender, a link that does not match its text.

Effective programmes are frequent, short and specific, and they make reporting easy and blame-free. A staff member who reports a click within minutes turns a breach into a contained incident.

Key points

  • Most breaches begin with a person, not a technical flaw.
  • Short, frequent training beats an annual lecture.
  • Teach recognition signals: urgency, authority, unexpected attachments, mismatched links.
  • Make reporting easy, fast and blame-free.
  • Simulated phishing measures the programme, if used to teach rather than punish.
  • Everyone is a target — executives and finance staff most of all.

Example

An employee clicks a phishing link, realises immediately, and reports it within two minutes. Credentials are reset before the attacker uses them. In an organisation that punishes clicks, that report never comes, and the account is used for weeks.

Why this matters

Awareness is the control that decides whether an incident is caught in minutes or discovered months later by someone outside the organisation.

lessons.title: 4.1 What Is Linux?
lessons.html:
📖 What Is Linux?
The operating system most servers and most security tools run on.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

What Is Linux?

What Is Linux? is the focus of this Linux for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use Linux confidently for defensive system administration and analysis.

Linux

An open-source family of operating systems.

terminal

A text interface used to enter commands.

permission

A rule controlling who may read, write, or execute a resource.

Linux is an open-source operating system family. Its kernel is shared; distributions such as Ubuntu, Debian and Kali package it differently for different purposes.

Security professionals need it because the majority of internet servers run it, most security tooling is built for it, and its logs and permissions model are what you will be investigating.

Key points

  • Linux is open source: the code is public and auditable.
  • Distributions share a kernel but differ in packaging and defaults.
  • Ubuntu and Debian are general purpose; Kali bundles security tooling.
  • Most web servers and cloud workloads run Linux.
  • Everything in Linux is represented as a file, including devices.
  • The command line is the primary interface for administration and investigation.

Example

A SOC analyst investigating a compromised web server will be reading Linux logs at a terminal, not clicking through a graphical interface. The skill is not optional in defensive security work.

Why this matters

Modules 5, 7, 9 and 11 all assume Linux familiarity, because that is where the logs, the tools and the evidence live.

lessons.title: 4.2 Installing a Linux Virtual Machine
lessons.html:
📖 Installing a Linux Virtual Machine
A disposable lab you can break safely.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Installing a Linux Virtual Machine

Installing a Linux Virtual Machine is the focus of this Linux for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use Linux confidently for defensive system administration and analysis.

Linux

An open-source family of operating systems.

terminal

A text interface used to enter commands.

permission

A rule controlling who may read, write, or execute a resource.

A virtual machine runs a complete operating system inside your existing one. For security practice this is essential: you get an isolated environment you can snapshot, break, and restore.

Use VirtualBox or VMware with an Ubuntu or Kali image. Take a snapshot once it is configured, so any experiment can be undone in seconds.

Key points

  • A VM isolates your practice environment from your real machine.
  • VirtualBox is free and sufficient for everything in this course.
  • Take a snapshot after setup so you can roll back instantly.
  • Allocate at least 2 GB RAM and 20 GB disk for a usable lab.
  • Use a host-only or NAT network when handling anything untrusted.
  • Never analyse suspicious files on your everyday machine.

Example

Analysing a suspicious file on your own laptop risks infecting it. Doing the same inside a snapshotted VM on an isolated network means the worst case is restoring a snapshot and losing five minutes.

Why this matters

Every practical exercise from here on assumes a lab you can safely break. Building it once removes the temptation to practise on systems that matter.

lessons.title: 4.3 Linux Terminal Basics
lessons.html:
📖 Linux Terminal Basics
A dozen commands cover most of what an analyst does.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Linux Terminal Basics

Linux Terminal Basics is the focus of this Linux for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use Linux confidently for defensive system administration and analysis.

Linux

An open-source family of operating systems.

terminal

A text interface used to enter commands.

permission

A rule controlling who may read, write, or execute a resource.

The terminal is where Linux administration and investigation happen. A small set of commands handles navigation, reading files and finding things — and those are most of what log analysis requires.

Commands take options and arguments: ls -la /var/log lists all files, in long form, in the log directory. The pattern is consistent across almost every command.

Key points

  • pwd where am I, ls list, cd change directory.
  • cat, less, head, tail read files; tail -f follows a live log.
  • grep searches text — the most used command in log analysis.
  • find locates files; man shows the manual for any command.
  • The pipe | sends one command's output into another.
  • Linux is case-sensitive: Log and log are different.

Example

grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | wc -l counts failed SSH logins. Two commands joined by a pipe answer a question that would take far longer in a graphical tool.

Why this matters

Log analysis in Modules 9 and 10 is largely grep, pipes and patience. These commands are the working vocabulary of the job.

lessons.title: 4.4 Linux File System
lessons.html:
📖 Linux File System
A single tree, and the security-relevant directories are few.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Linux File System

Linux File System is the focus of this Linux for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use Linux confidently for defensive system administration and analysis.

Linux

An open-source family of operating systems.

terminal

A text interface used to enter commands.

permission

A rule controlling who may read, write, or execute a resource.

Linux has one directory tree starting at /. There are no drive letters; storage devices are mounted into the tree. Knowing which directories matter narrows an investigation quickly.

For an analyst the important ones are /var/log (logs), /etc (configuration), /home (user data), /tmp (world-writable temporary space, a favourite for dropped malware).

Key points

  • Everything hangs off the root directory /.
  • /var/log — system and application logs; the analyst's first stop.
  • /etc — configuration, including users and services.
  • /home — user files; /root is the administrator's home.
  • /tmp is world-writable, so malicious files often appear there.
  • Files beginning with a dot are hidden; ls -la reveals them.

Example

An executable file in /tmp with a random name, owned by the web server account, is a strong indicator of compromise. Both the location and the owner are wrong for a legitimate binary.

Why this matters

Knowing the tree turns “search the whole server” into “check four directories”, which is the difference between an investigation that finishes and one that does not.

lessons.title: 4.5 Users and Permissions
lessons.html:
📖 Users and Permissions
Read, write, execute — for owner, group and everyone else.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Users and Permissions

Users and Permissions is the focus of this Linux for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use Linux confidently for defensive system administration and analysis.

Linux

An open-source family of operating systems.

terminal

A text interface used to enter commands.

permission

A rule controlling who may read, write, or execute a resource.

Every Linux file has an owner, a group, and three permission sets. rwxr-xr-- means the owner may read, write and execute; the group may read and execute; everyone else may only read.

Numeric notation is the same thing: read is 4, write is 2, execute is 1. So 755 is rwx for owner, r-x for group and others, and 777 — writable by everyone — is almost always a mistake.

Key points

  • Three sets: owner, group, others.
  • read = 4, write = 2, execute = 1; add them per set.
  • 755 is a normal executable; 644 a normal file; 777 is a red flag.
  • chmod changes permissions; chown changes ownership.
  • SUID files run with the owner's privileges — a classic escalation route.
  • /etc/passwd lists accounts; /etc/shadow holds password hashes and must not be world-readable.

Example

Finding /etc/shadow world-readable means every account's password hash can be copied by any user on the system, and cracked offline at leisure. One permission bit, total credential exposure.

Why this matters

Permission review is a standard hardening task and a standard forensic check, and SUID misconfiguration is one of the most common privilege escalation findings in real assessments.

lessons.title: 4.6 Managing Processes
lessons.html:
📖 Managing Processes
Seeing what is running is the first step of every incident.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Managing Processes

Managing Processes is the focus of this Linux for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use Linux confidently for defensive system administration and analysis.

Linux

An open-source family of operating systems.

terminal

A text interface used to enter commands.

permission

A rule controlling who may read, write, or execute a resource.

Linux tools show running processes, who owns them, what started them and what they are doing. ps aux lists everything; top shows live resource use; systemctl manages services.

During an investigation you are looking for the same anomalies as on any system: unexpected owners, odd paths, strange parent processes, and unusual network activity from a process that should not have any.

Key points

  • ps aux lists all processes with owner, PID and command line.
  • top or htop shows live CPU and memory use.
  • systemctl manages services; check for unfamiliar enabled units.
  • ss -tulpn shows which process is listening on which port.
  • kill stops a process by PID; capture evidence before you do.
  • Check the parent process — a shell spawned by a web server is a red flag.

Example

ss -tulpn shows a process listening on port 4444 owned by the web server account. A web server should serve on 80 and 443 and listen on nothing else. That single line justifies isolating the host.

Why this matters

This is the practical core of Linux incident response: what is running, who owns it, what started it, and what is it talking to.

lessons.title: 4.7 Installing Software
lessons.html:
📖 Installing Software
Package managers are a security control, not just a convenience.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Installing Software

Installing Software is the focus of this Linux for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use Linux confidently for defensive system administration and analysis.

Linux

An open-source family of operating systems.

terminal

A text interface used to enter commands.

permission

A rule controlling who may read, write, or execute a resource.

Linux software is installed from repositories using a package manager: apt on Debian and Ubuntu, dnf or yum on Red Hat family systems. Packages are signed, and the manager verifies those signatures.

That verification is the point. Downloading a binary from a website and running it bypasses every integrity guarantee the distribution provides — and is a common way systems get compromised.

Key points

  • apt update refreshes the package list; apt upgrade applies updates.
  • Repository packages are signed and verified on install.
  • Adding an untrusted third-party repository extends trust to its owner.
  • Never pipe a script from the internet straight into a shell without reading it.
  • Patching is the single highest-value maintenance task for security.
  • Remove packages you do not use — each one is attack surface.

Example

curl example.com/install.sh | bash executes whatever that server returns, at that moment, with your privileges, unreviewed. If the site is compromised between your two visits, so are you.

Why this matters

Unpatched software and untrusted installs are two of the most common root causes in real incidents, and both are addressed by using the package manager properly.

lessons.title: 4.8 Networking Commands
lessons.html:
📖 Networking Commands
Six commands answer most network questions from a Linux host.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Networking Commands

Networking Commands is the focus of this Linux for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use Linux confidently for defensive system administration and analysis.

Linux

An open-source family of operating systems.

terminal

A text interface used to enter commands.

permission

A rule controlling who may read, write, or execute a resource.

Linux ships with everything needed to check connectivity, resolve names, inspect connections and trace paths. These are the same commands used for troubleshooting and for investigation.

In an incident they answer specific questions: what is this host connected to, what name does that address resolve to, and can it reach the outside world at all?

Key points

  • ip a shows interfaces and addresses.
  • ping tests reachability; traceroute shows the path.
  • dig or nslookup resolves DNS names.
  • ss -tunap lists current connections with their processes.
  • curl -I fetches HTTP headers without downloading a page.
  • tcpdump captures packets for detailed analysis.

Example

During an investigation, ss -tunap reveals an established connection to a foreign address, and dig -x on that address returns a hosting provider with no business relationship to the organisation. Two commands, one clear lead.

Why this matters

These commands are how you confirm or dismiss a network alert from the host itself, rather than trusting a dashboard.

lessons.title: 4.9 Bash Fundamentals
lessons.html:
📖 Bash Fundamentals
Scripting turns a repeated investigation into one command.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Bash Fundamentals

Bash Fundamentals is the focus of this Linux for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use Linux confidently for defensive system administration and analysis.

Linux

An open-source family of operating systems.

terminal

A text interface used to enter commands.

permission

A rule controlling who may read, write, or execute a resource.

Bash is the default Linux shell and its scripting language. For security work it automates the repetitive parts: collecting the same evidence from several hosts, parsing logs the same way each time, checking configurations.

A script is a file of commands with #!/bin/bash on the first line, made executable with chmod +x. Variables, conditions and loops are all you need for most security automation.

Key points

  • Start scripts with #!/bin/bash and make them executable.
  • Variables: name=value, used as $name.
  • Loops repeat over files or lines; conditions branch on results.
  • $? holds the previous command's exit status — 0 means success.
  • Quote variables ("$file") so spaces and odd characters do not break the script.
  • Never run an unread script, and never store credentials inside one.

Example

A five-line loop that runs the same four evidence-collection commands across twenty hosts turns an hour of manual work into a minute — and, more importantly, collects exactly the same data from every host.

Why this matters

Consistency is the real benefit. Manual collection varies between hosts and analysts; a script does not, which matters when the output becomes evidence.

lessons.title: 4.10 Linux Security Basics
lessons.html:
📖 Linux Security Basics
Hardening is mostly removing things.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Linux Security Basics

Linux Security Basics is the focus of this Linux for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use Linux confidently for defensive system administration and analysis.

Linux

An open-source family of operating systems.

terminal

A text interface used to enter commands.

permission

A rule controlling who may read, write, or execute a resource.

Securing a Linux host comes down to a short list: patch it, remove what you do not need, restrict who may log in and how, enforce least privilege, and make sure it is logging.

SSH deserves particular attention because it is the usual remote access route. Disable root login, prefer key authentication over passwords, and never expose it to the whole internet without restriction.

Key points

  • Patch regularly — unpatched services are the most common entry point.
  • Disable unused services; every listening port is attack surface.
  • SSH: disable root login, use key authentication, restrict source addresses.
  • Enforce least privilege and audit sudo rights.
  • Enable a host firewall (ufw or firewalld).
  • Ensure logging is on and shipped off the host, so an attacker cannot erase it.

Example

A server with password SSH open to the internet receives thousands of login attempts a day. Switching to key authentication makes those attempts pointless overnight, without blocking a single legitimate user.

Why this matters

These few measures remove most of the routes by which Linux servers are actually compromised, and shipping logs off-host is what preserves the evidence when one is.

lessons.title: 5.1 What Is Ethical Hacking?
lessons.html:
📖 What Is Ethical Hacking?
Testing defences with permission, to fix what you find.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

What Is Ethical Hacking?

What Is Ethical Hacking? is the focus of this Ethical Hacking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to assess security only with explicit authorization and document findings responsibly.

ethical hacking

Authorized security testing performed to improve protection.

scope

The systems, methods, and limits approved for an assessment.

vulnerability

A weakness that could be exploited to cause harm.

Ethical hacking is authorised security testing. The techniques overlap with attack; what makes it lawful and professional is written authorisation, an agreed scope, and a report that helps the owner fix the findings.

Without those three, the same activity is a criminal offence in most jurisdictions, including Liberia. The distinction is not technical — it is documentary.

Key points

  • Authorisation must be written and obtained before any testing.
  • Scope defines which systems, which techniques, and which times.
  • The deliverable is a report that enables remediation, not a trophy.
  • Penetration test: authorised, goal-driven. Vulnerability assessment: breadth-first scanning.
  • Testing outside scope voids the authorisation for that activity.
  • Bug bounty programmes are authorisation published in advance — read the rules.

Example

A tester finds a vulnerability in a system adjacent to the agreed scope. The professional response is to report the observation and request scope extension in writing — not to test it because it was interesting.

Why this matters

This module teaches the assessment process. Every technique in it is only legitimate inside the authorisation that this lesson describes.

questions.explanation: The purpose is improving the client's security, which requires actionable reporting.

lessons.title: 5.2 Legal and Ethical Responsibilities
lessons.html:
📖 Legal and Ethical Responsibilities
Know the law before you run the tool.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Legal and Ethical Responsibilities

Legal and Ethical Responsibilities is the focus of this Ethical Hacking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to assess security only with explicit authorization and document findings responsibly.

ethical hacking

Authorized security testing performed to improve protection.

scope

The systems, methods, and limits approved for an assessment.

vulnerability

A weakness that could be exploited to cause harm.

Unauthorised access to a computer system is a criminal offence in most countries. Testing a system you do not own, without permission, exposes you to prosecution regardless of your intent or whether you caused damage.

Professional obligations go beyond legality: handle any data you encounter confidentially, minimise disruption, report findings responsibly, and stop when the scope says stop.

Key points

  • Unauthorised access is a criminal offence in most jurisdictions.
  • Good intentions are not a legal defence.
  • Keep the signed authorisation available for the duration of testing.
  • Treat any data you encounter as confidential; do not exfiltrate it.
  • Practise only on your own lab, or on platforms that exist for the purpose.
  • Disclose findings responsibly — to the owner first, with time to fix.

Example

Scanning a company's website “to see if it is secure” without asking is unauthorised access. That it revealed a real flaw, and that you meant to help, does not change the legal position.

Why this matters

This is the lesson that protects your career. Technical skill without this discipline ends in prosecution rather than employment.
