lessons.title: 5.3 Reconnaissance
lessons.html:
📖 Reconnaissance
Understanding a target before testing it — mostly from public sources.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Reconnaissance

Reconnaissance is the focus of this Ethical Hacking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to assess security only with explicit authorization and document findings responsibly.

ethical hacking

Authorized security testing performed to improve protection.

scope

The systems, methods, and limits approved for an assessment.

vulnerability

A weakness that could be exploited to cause harm.

Reconnaissance is the information-gathering phase. Passive reconnaissance uses public sources and never touches the target. Active reconnaissance interacts with it and therefore requires authorisation.

Defensively, this is worth understanding because it tells you what attackers can learn about your organisation for free — and what you should therefore stop publishing.

Key points

  • Passive: public records, DNS data, job adverts, social media, certificate logs.
  • Active: any interaction with the target — needs authorisation.
  • Job adverts reveal internal technologies with unhelpful precision.
  • Certificate transparency logs expose subdomain names publicly.
  • Employee social media reveals names, roles and email address formats.
  • Defensive lesson: review what your organisation publishes.

Example

A job advert for “an administrator experienced with a specific VPN appliance and version” tells an attacker exactly which product to research for known vulnerabilities. Nobody needed to touch the network to learn it.

Why this matters

Attack surface reduction starts with knowing what is publicly visible. Most organisations are surprised by how much that is.

lessons.html:
📖 Information Gathering
Turning scattered public data into a picture of the attack surface.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Information Gathering

Information Gathering is the focus of this Ethical Hacking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to assess security only with explicit authorization and document findings responsibly.

Authorized security testing performed to improve protection.

scope

The systems, methods, and limits approved for an assessment.

vulnerability

A weakness that could be exploited to cause harm.

Information gathering organises what reconnaissance finds: which domains and subdomains exist, which addresses they resolve to, which services answer, and which technologies are in use.

For defenders this is attack surface management — and the most common finding is assets nobody remembered owning: a forgotten test server, an old subdomain, a service left running after a project ended.

Key points

  • Enumerate domains, subdomains, addresses and exposed services.
  • Forgotten assets are the most common serious finding.
  • Certificate transparency logs list subdomains you may have forgotten.
  • Maintain an asset inventory — you cannot defend what you do not know you own.
  • Identify technology versions to check them against known vulnerabilities.
  • Repeat periodically; attack surface grows quietly.

Example

A subdomain enumeration turns up old-test.example.com, running a three-year-old application that nobody has patched because nobody remembered it existed. It is reachable from the internet.

Why this matters

Asset inventory sounds administrative and is genuinely one of the highest-value security controls, because forgotten systems are unpatched systems.

lessons.title: 5.5 Vulnerability Scanning
lessons.html:
📖 Vulnerability Scanning
Automated checking for known weaknesses — and the results always need a human.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Vulnerability Scanning

Vulnerability Scanning is the focus of this Ethical Hacking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to assess security only with explicit authorization and document findings responsibly.

ethical hacking

Authorized security testing performed to improve protection.

scope

The systems, methods, and limits approved for an assessment.

vulnerability

A weakness that could be exploited to cause harm.

A vulnerability scanner compares what it finds against a database of known issues and reports matches with severity ratings. It is broad and fast, and it is not a penetration test.

Scanner output requires validation. False positives waste remediation effort; false negatives create false confidence. Severity ratings also ignore your context: a critical finding on an isolated system may matter less than a medium one on an internet-facing server.

Key points

  • Scanners detect known vulnerabilities from a signature database.
  • CVE identifies a vulnerability; CVSS scores its severity.
  • Always validate findings — false positives are common.
  • Severity is not priority: exposure and data sensitivity change the ranking.
  • Authenticated scans see far more than unauthenticated ones.
  • Scanning production systems can disrupt them — agree timing in advance.

Example

A scanner reports 400 findings. Fourteen are on internet-facing systems holding customer data; the rest are on an isolated test network. The fourteen are the work. Treating all 400 as equal guarantees the fourteen are not fixed first.

Why this matters

Vulnerability management is a large part of real security work, and the skill is prioritisation rather than scanning.

lessons.title: 5.6 Network Scanning

📖 Network Scanning
Discovering which hosts exist and which services they expose.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Network Scanning

Network Scanning is the focus of this Ethical Hacking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to assess security only with explicit authorization and document findings responsibly.

ethical hacking

Authorized security testing performed to improve protection.

scope

The systems, methods, and limits approved for an assessment.

vulnerability

A weakness that could be exploited to cause harm.

Network scanning identifies live hosts, open ports and the services behind them. It is the standard first technical step in an authorised assessment, and the standard first step in an attack — which is why detecting it matters.

Scans are noisy. From the defensive side, a burst of connection attempts across many ports or many hosts from one source is one of the clearest signals available in firewall logs.

Key points

  • Host discovery finds live systems; port scanning finds open services.
  • Service and version detection identifies what is actually listening.
  • Scanning requires authorisation — it is an interaction with the target.
  • Aggressive scans can disrupt fragile services; agree timing beforehand.
  • Defensively, sequential connection attempts across ports are a scan signature.
  • Internal scanning after a compromise is a strong lateral movement indicator.

Example

Firewall logs show one internal address attempting connections to 300 different ports on 40 hosts within two minutes. No legitimate application behaves that way. That pattern is why scan detection is a standard SOC rule.

Why this matters

Understanding what a scan looks like from both sides is what lets an analyst recognise the reconnaissance stage of an intrusion while it is still reconnaissance.

lessons.title: 5.7 Understanding Common Vulnerabilities
lessons.html:
📖 Understanding Common Vulnerabilities
A handful of root causes explain most findings.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Understanding Common Vulnerabilities

Understanding Common Vulnerabilities is the focus of this Ethical Hacking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to assess security only with explicit authorization and document findings responsibly.

ethical hacking

Authorized security testing performed to improve protection.

scope

The systems, methods, and limits approved for an assessment.

vulnerability

A weakness that could be exploited to cause harm.

Most vulnerabilities trace back to a few causes: missing patches, weak or default configuration, insufficient input validation, broken access control, and exposed services that should not be reachable.

Knowing the root cause matters more than memorising individual issues, because the fix follows from the cause and the same cause recurs across different products.

Key points

  • Missing patches — known flaws left unfixed; the most common root cause.
  • Default configuration — default credentials, sample content, verbose errors.
  • Insufficient input validation — the root of injection flaws.
  • Broken access control — checks missing or enforced only client-side.
  • Unnecessary exposure — management interfaces reachable from the internet.
  • Zero-day means no patch exists yet; it is rarer than headlines suggest.

Example

A database administration console reachable from the internet with its default password is not a sophisticated vulnerability. It is three ordinary mistakes stacked together, and it is how a great many breaches actually begin.

Why this matters

Categorising by root cause tells you what to fix systematically rather than chasing individual findings one at a time.

lessons.title: 5.8 Web Security Fundamentals
lessons.html:
📖 Web Security Fundamentals
Web applications are the largest attack surface most organisations have.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Web Security Fundamentals

Web Security Fundamentals is the focus of this Ethical Hacking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to assess security only with explicit authorization and document findings responsibly.

ethical hacking

Authorized security testing performed to improve protection.

scope

The systems, methods, and limits approved for an assessment.

vulnerability

A weakness that could be exploited to cause harm.

Web applications are reachable by anyone, accept untrusted input by design, and often hold the organisation's most valuable data. That combination is why they dominate breach statistics.

The foundational rule is simple to state and hard to apply consistently: never trust input, and enforce every security decision on the server, where the user cannot alter it.

Key points

  • All client-supplied input is untrusted, including headers and cookies.
  • Enforce authentication and authorisation server-side, always.
  • Validate input by allow-list where possible, not by blocking known-bad.
  • Encode output for the context it is rendered into.
  • Use HTTPS everywhere; mixed content undermines the protection.
  • Error messages should not disclose stack traces, versions or queries.

Example

A page hides an administrative button from ordinary users in the browser. The underlying endpoint has no server-side check. Anyone who guesses the URL becomes an administrator — the control was decoration.

Why this matters

Module 6 covers these issues individually; this lesson is the principle they all reduce to.

lessons.title: 5.9 Password Security Testing
lessons.html:
📖 Password Security Testing
Assessing credential strength as part of an authorised assessment.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Password Security Testing

Password Security Testing is the focus of this Ethical Hacking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to assess security only with explicit authorization and document findings responsibly.

ethical hacking

Authorized security testing performed to improve protection.

scope

The systems, methods, and limits approved for an assessment.

vulnerability

A weakness that could be exploited to cause harm.

Within an authorised engagement, testers assess whether an organisation's credentials would resist attack: are default passwords still in place, are accounts reused, would the stored hashes fall quickly to offline cracking?

This is done against systems in scope, with the client's knowledge, and the results are reported as a policy weakness rather than a list of individual people's passwords.

Key points

  • Only ever performed under written authorisation and defined scope.
  • Check first for default and vendor credentials — the commonest finding.
  • Offline hash analysis avoids account lockouts and service disruption.
  • Report patterns and policy gaps, not individual users' passwords.
  • Weak hashing (unsalted, fast algorithms) is itself the finding to report.
  • Recommend MFA, length-based policy and a password manager, not forced rotation.

Example

A test finds 40% of hashes recovered quickly because the application stored them unsalted with a fast algorithm. The finding is the storage method, which is fixable centrally, rather than forty individual weak passwords.

Why this matters

Framing the result as a systemic weakness rather than a list of people is what makes the report actionable and keeps the exercise professional.

lessons.title: 5.10 Writing a Security Assessment
lessons.html:
📖 Writing a Security Assessment
The report is the product; everything before it is preparation.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Writing a Security Assessment

Writing a Security Assessment is the focus of this Ethical Hacking Fundamentals lesson. It develops the learner's ability to assess security only with explicit authorization and document findings responsibly.

ethical hacking

Authorized security testing performed to improve protection.

scope

The systems, methods, and limits approved for an assessment.

vulnerability

A weakness that could be exploited to cause harm.

A security assessment report has to be usable by two audiences: management, who need the risk and the decision, and technical staff, who need enough detail to reproduce and fix the issue.

Each finding should state what it is, where it was found, how it was verified, what the business impact is, and precisely what to do about it. Findings without reproduction steps get disputed; findings without remediation advice get deferred.

Key points

  • Open with an executive summary in business language, not technical detail.
  • Each finding: description, location, evidence, impact, remediation, severity.
  • Include reproduction steps — a finding that cannot be reproduced gets dismissed.
  • Rate by business risk, not scanner severity alone.
  • Give specific remediation, not “apply best practice”.
  • Handle the report itself as confidential — it is a map of the weaknesses.

Example

“SQL injection found” is not a finding. “SQL injection in the search parameter of /products, verified by an error-based payload, exposing the product database; fix by using parameterised queries” is one the developer can act on this week.

Why this matters

Reporting is the most transferable skill in this module. It is also the one that most often separates a tester who is rehired from one who is not.

lessons.title: 6.1 How Websites Work
lessons.html:
📖 How Websites Work
Request, response, and where the security decisions actually happen.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

How Websites Work

How Websites Work is the focus of this Web Application Security lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and defend web applications against common weaknesses.

web application

Software accessed through a web browser or web protocol.

session

Server-maintained state connecting multiple user requests.

input validation

Checking data before processing it.

A browser sends an HTTP request; a server returns a response. The front end runs in the browser, under the user's control. The back end runs on the server, under yours.

Every security control must live on the back end. Anything the browser enforces — hidden fields, disabled buttons, client-side validation — can be changed by anyone who opens the developer tools.

Key points

  • Front end runs in the browser and is fully controllable by the user.
  • Back end runs on the server and is where security must be enforced.
  • HTTP is stateless; sessions add continuity between requests.
  • Client-side validation improves usability, never security.
  • Web servers, application code and databases each produce useful logs.
  • Every request is an opportunity for untrusted input to enter.

Example

A checkout page validates the price in JavaScript. A user edits the value in the browser and submits a price of 1. The server accepts it because it never re-checked. The validation was a convenience, not a control.

Why this matters

This single distinction — who controls which side — explains almost every web vulnerability in this module.

lessons.title: 6.2 HTTP and HTTPS
lessons.html:
📖 HTTP and HTTPS
The same protocol, with and without a protective layer.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

HTTP and HTTPS

HTTP and HTTPS is the focus of this Web Application Security lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and defend web applications against common weaknesses.

web application

Software accessed through a web browser or web protocol.

session

Server-maintained state connecting multiple user requests.

input validation

Checking data before processing it.

HTTP carries requests and responses in plain text. HTTPS wraps it in TLS, encrypting the content and authenticating the server's domain name.

Without HTTPS, anyone positioned on the network path can read and modify the traffic. With it, they see only that a connection occurred and to which host.

Key points

  • HTTP is plain text; HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS.
  • Methods: GET retrieves, POST submits; GET parameters appear in logs and history.
  • Status codes: 200 success, 301/302 redirect, 401/403 auth failures, 404 not found, 500 server error.
  • TLS proves the domain, not the honesty of its operator.
  • HSTS forces browsers to use HTTPS and blocks downgrade attempts.
  • Security headers matter: HSTS, Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options.

Example

Sending credentials over HTTP on shared Wi-Fi exposes them to anyone on that network. The same login over HTTPS exposes only the fact that a connection to that site occurred.

Why this matters

Status codes and headers are also detection signals: a burst of 401s is a brute-force attempt, and a burst of 500s often means someone is probing for injection flaws.

lessons.title: 6.3 Cookies and Sessions
lessons.html:
📖 Cookies and Sessions
How a stateless protocol remembers who you are — and how that gets stolen.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Cookies and Sessions

Cookies and Sessions is the focus of this Web Application Security lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and defend web applications against common weaknesses.

web application

Software accessed through a web browser or web protocol.

session

Server-maintained state connecting multiple user requests.

input validation

Checking data before processing it.

After login, the server issues a session identifier, usually in a cookie. The browser returns it with every subsequent request, and the server uses it to recognise the user.

That token is therefore equivalent to the password for the duration of the session. Session hijacking — stealing the token — skips authentication entirely, including MFA.

Key points

  • A session token identifies the user for the life of the session.
  • HttpOnly stops JavaScript reading the cookie, blunting XSS theft.
  • Secure sends it only over HTTPS.
  • SameSite limits cross-site sending, mitigating CSRF.
  • Regenerate the session identifier on login to prevent session fixation.
  • Expire sessions, and invalidate them server-side on logout.

Example

A stolen session cookie logs an attacker straight in as the user. MFA was satisfied when the session was created, so it is never asked for again — which is why cookie protection flags matter as much as the login itself.

Why this matters

Session handling connects directly to XSS and CSRF later in this module: both are, in practice, ways of abusing someone else's session.

lessons.title: 6.4 Authentication Security
lessons.html:
📖 Authentication Security
Getting login right involves more than checking a password.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Authentication Security

Authentication Security is the focus of this Web Application Security lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and defend web applications against common weaknesses.

web application

Software accessed through a web browser or web protocol.

session

Server-maintained state connecting multiple user requests.

input validation

Checking data before processing it.

Secure authentication requires safe credential storage, rate limiting, careful error handling, secure session creation, and a password reset flow that cannot itself be abused.

Reset flows are frequently the weakest part. A predictable token, a link that never expires, or a response that reveals whether an account exists all undermine an otherwise solid login.

Key points

  • Store passwords as salted hashes using a slow algorithm (bcrypt, Argon2).
  • Rate limit and progressively delay repeated failures.
  • Return the same message whether the username or the password was wrong.
  • Reset tokens must be random, single-use and short-lived.
  • Do not reveal whether an account exists — that is user enumeration.
  • Support MFA, and re-authenticate before sensitive changes.

Example

“No account with that email” versus “Incorrect password” tells an attacker which addresses are registered. They can then focus their guessing on accounts that certainly exist.

Why this matters

Authentication is the front door of every application, and these details are what an assessment checks first because they are so often wrong.

lessons.title: 6.5 Access Control
lessons.html:
📖 Access Control
Checking permission on every request, not just on the first one.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Access Control

Access Control is the focus of this Web Application Security lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and defend web applications against common weaknesses.

web application

Software accessed through a web browser or web protocol.

session

Server-maintained state connecting multiple user requests.

input validation

Checking data before processing it.

Access control decides whether an authenticated user may perform a particular action on a particular object. It must be evaluated on the server, for every request, against the identity making it.

The classic failure is insecure direct object reference: the application checks that you are logged in, but not that the record you asked for is yours.

Key points

  • Check authorisation on every request, not only at login.
  • Verify object ownership, not merely that the user is authenticated.
  • Deny by default; grant explicitly.
  • Hiding a control in the interface is not access control.
  • Enforce for APIs exactly as for pages — APIs are often forgotten.
  • Log authorisation failures; repeated denials are an enumeration signal.

Example

Changing /invoice?id=1043 to /invoice?id=1044 returns another customer's invoice. The user was authenticated, so the login worked. Nobody checked that invoice 1044 belonged to them.

Why this matters

Broken access control is consistently the most frequently found serious category in real web assessments, and the OWASP Top 10 ranks it first.

lessons.title: 6.6 SQL Injection Concepts
lessons.html:
📖 SQL Injection Concepts
The database cannot tell your data apart from your instructions — unless you tell it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

SQL Injection Concepts

SQL Injection Concepts is the focus of this Web Application Security lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and defend web applications against common weaknesses.

web application

Software accessed through a web browser or web protocol.

session

Server-maintained state connecting multiple user requests.

input validation

Checking data before processing it.

SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into a database query, so the input can change what the query means rather than merely what it searches for. The consequences range from reading other users' data to bypassing login entirely.

The fix is not filtering. It is parameterised queries (prepared statements), which send the query structure and the data separately, so input can never be interpreted as SQL.

Key points

  • Cause: untrusted input concatenated into a query string.
  • Fix: parameterised queries in every query, without exception.
  • Blocklists and escaping are fragile and repeatedly bypassed.
  • Apply least privilege to the database account — the app rarely needs DROP.
  • Verbose database errors help attackers map the schema; return generic errors.
  • A WAF is a useful extra layer, never a substitute for parameterisation.

Example

Building a query as "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + input + "'" lets input close the quote and append its own clause. Using a parameter placeholder instead means the input is only ever compared as a value.

Why this matters

Injection has been in the OWASP Top 10 since it began, and the defence has been the same throughout. Knowing the cause makes the fix obvious.

lessons.title: 6.7 Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
lessons.html:
📖 Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
Getting the victim's browser to run the attacker's script.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) is the focus of this Web Application Security lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and defend web applications against common weaknesses.

web application

Software accessed through a web browser or web protocol.

session

Server-maintained state connecting multiple user requests.

input validation

Checking data before processing it.

XSS occurs when an application includes untrusted input in a page without encoding it, so the browser executes it as script. Because the script runs in the victim's session, it can read the page, steal tokens, or act as the user.

There are three forms: stored (saved on the server and served to others), reflected (bounced back from a request), and DOM-based (introduced by client-side code).

Key points

  • Cause: untrusted input rendered into a page without contextual encoding.
  • Stored XSS affects every viewer; it is the most damaging form.
  • Reflected XSS needs the victim to follow a crafted link.
  • Fix: encode output for its context — HTML, attribute, JavaScript, URL.
  • Content-Security-Policy limits what scripts may run.
  • HttpOnly cookies stop script reading session tokens.

Example

A comment field that stores input unencoded means every visitor's browser runs whatever the last commenter wrote. One malicious comment reaches every reader — which is why stored XSS is rated above reflected.

Why this matters

XSS is the practical route to session hijacking, tying this lesson directly back to the cookie protections covered earlier in the module.

lessons.title: 6.8 Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
lessons.html:
📖 Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
Making the victim's browser send a request it did not intend.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)

Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) is the focus of this Web Application Security lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and defend web applications against common weaknesses.

web application

Software accessed through a web browser or web protocol.

session

Server-maintained state connecting multiple user requests.

input validation

Checking data before processing it.

CSRF abuses the fact that browsers attach cookies automatically. A page under the attacker's control causes the victim's browser to submit a request to a site where the victim is logged in, and that site accepts it as legitimate.

The defence is to require something the attacker's page cannot supply: an unpredictable anti-CSRF token tied to the session, backed by the SameSite cookie attribute.

Key points

  • Cause: browsers send cookies automatically with cross-site requests.
  • The attacker cannot read the response — CSRF causes actions, not disclosure.
  • Fix: per-session anti-CSRF tokens on every state-changing request.
  • SameSite=Lax or Strict blocks most cross-site cookie sending.
  • Never perform state changes on a GET request.
  • Re-authenticate before genuinely sensitive actions such as changing an email.

Example

A victim visits a malicious page while logged into their bank in another tab. The page silently submits a transfer form. The bank sees a properly authenticated request — the browser attached the session cookie without being asked.

Why this matters

CSRF is why state-changing operations should never be reachable by GET, and why SameSite became a browser default.

lessons.title: 6.9 Secure Web Development
lessons.html:
📖 Secure Web Development
Building security in costs far less than adding it afterwards.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Secure Web Development

Secure Web Development is the focus of this Web Application Security lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and defend web applications against common weaknesses.

web application

Software accessed through a web browser or web protocol.

session

Server-maintained state connecting multiple user requests.

input validation

Checking data before processing it.

Secure development means applying the same few principles consistently: validate input, encode output, enforce authorisation server-side, manage secrets properly, and keep dependencies current.

Most real vulnerabilities are not exotic. They come from doing one of these five things inconsistently — usually in the one endpoint that was added in a hurry.

Key points

  • Validate input by allow-list; encode output by context.
  • Enforce authorisation server-side on every request, including APIs.
  • Keep secrets out of source code and out of the repository.
  • Track and update dependencies — most code in an app is not yours.
  • Log security-relevant events, and never log credentials or tokens.
  • Review code and test before release, not after an incident.

Example

An API key committed to a public repository is compromised the moment it is pushed, and rotating it is the only remedy. Automated scanners find such keys within minutes of publication.

Why this matters

Consistency is what matters here. One endpoint that skips the authorisation check undoes the work done on every other endpoint.

lessons.title: 6.10 OWASP Top 10
lessons.html:
📖 OWASP Top 10
The industry's shared list of what actually goes wrong.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

OWASP Top 10

OWASP Top 10 is the focus of this Web Application Security lesson. It develops the learner's ability to understand and defend web applications against common weaknesses.

web application

Software accessed through a web browser or web protocol.

session

Server-maintained state connecting multiple user requests.

input validation

Checking data before processing it.

The OWASP Top 10 is a periodically updated, community-produced list of the most critical web application security risks. It is used as a baseline in testing, in development standards and in compliance requirements.

It is a starting point rather than a complete standard. Passing a Top 10 review does not mean an application is secure; failing one almost certainly means it is not.

Key points

  • Broken Access Control currently ranks first.
  • Cryptographic Failures — weak or missing protection of data.
  • Injection — including SQL injection and XSS.
  • Insecure Design — flaws no amount of coding care can fix later.
  • Security Misconfiguration — defaults, verbose errors, open storage.
  • Also: vulnerable components, authentication failures, integrity failures, logging failures, SSRF.

Example

The list is derived from data across many organisations, so it reflects what is actually found rather than what is theoretically interesting. Broken access control tops it because it is found most often, not because it is the most sophisticated.

Why this matters

The Top 10 gives you a shared vocabulary with developers and auditors, and it is asked about in almost every security interview.

lessons.title: 7.1 Introduction to Python
lessons.html:
📖 Introduction to Python
The language security work is written in.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Introduction to Python

Introduction to Python is the focus of this Python for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to write understandable Python programs for safe security automation.

variable

A named reference to a stored value.

function

A reusable block of code that performs a defined task.

automation

Use of software to perform repeatable work consistently.

Python is readable, quick to write, and has libraries for almost everything a security task needs: parsing logs, calling APIs, handling network data, working with files.

You do not need to become a software engineer. Security automation is usually fifty lines that read a file, look for a pattern, and produce a summary — and that is a realistic skill to reach in a few weeks.

Key points

  • Python is interpreted, so you run scripts directly without compiling.
  • Indentation defines code blocks — it is syntax, not style.
  • The standard library already covers files, JSON, regular expressions and HTTP.
  • Most security tooling offers a Python interface.
  • Readable code matters: security scripts are read by other analysts.
  • Comment why, not what — the code already says what.

Example

A twenty-line script that reads an authentication log, counts failures per source address, and prints anything over a threshold replaces a manual task an analyst would otherwise repeat every morning.

Why this matters

Everything in this module builds toward that: small, reliable tools that remove repetitive work and make analysis consistent.

lessons.title: 7.2 Installing Python
lessons.html:
📖 Installing Python
Set it up once, with a virtual environment, and avoid a common class of problem.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Installing Python

Installing Python is the focus of this Python for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to write understandable Python programs for safe security automation.

variable

A named reference to a stored value.

function

A reusable block of code that performs a defined task.

automation

Use of software to perform repeatable work consistently.

Install Python from python.org or through your Linux package manager. Most Linux systems already have Python 3 available. Verify with python3 --version.

Use a virtual environment for each project. It keeps each project's dependencies separate, so installing a package for one tool cannot break another — and it avoids installing packages system-wide as root.

Key points

  • Python 3 is the current version; Python 2 is retired and unsupported.
  • python3 -m venv .venv creates a virtual environment.
  • Activate it before installing packages with pip.
  • Never sudo pip install — it pollutes the system Python.
  • pip freeze > requirements.txt records exact versions for reproducibility.
  • Review packages before installing; typosquatted package names are a real attack.

Example

Installing a package whose name is one letter off a popular library can execute code at install time. Package name typosquatting is a live supply chain attack, and reading the name carefully is the whole defence.

Why this matters

A clean environment per project prevents the dependency conflicts that otherwise consume more time than the security work itself.

lessons.title: 7.3 Python Variables and Data Types
lessons.html:
📖 Python Variables and Data Types
The few types that carry almost all security data.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Python Variables and Data Types

Python Variables and Data Types is the focus of this Python for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to write understandable Python programs for safe security automation.

variable

A named reference to a stored value.

function

A reusable block of code that performs a defined task.

automation

Use of software to perform repeatable work consistently.

Python's core types are strings, integers, floats, booleans, lists and dictionaries. Log analysis mostly means strings and dictionaries; counting and thresholds mean integers.

A dictionary maps keys to values and is the natural structure for security data: an IP address to a count, a username to a list of events, a field name to its value.

Key points

  • str text, int whole numbers, float decimals, bool true/false.
  • list is an ordered collection; dict maps keys to values.
  • Types are dynamic but not interchangeable: "5" + 5 is an error.
  • JSON maps directly onto dictionaries and lists, which is why APIs are easy.
  • set holds unique values — ideal for deduplicating addresses.
  • Convert explicitly with int(), str() and float().

Example

Counting failed logins per address is a dictionary: the key is the address, the value is the count. Adding a source is one line, and the result is already in the shape a report needs.

Why this matters

Choosing the right structure is most of the work. A dictionary turns a counting problem into three lines; a list turns it into fifteen.

lessons.title: 7.4 Conditions and Loops
lessons.html:
📖 Conditions and Loops
Decide and repeat — the two things every analysis script does.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Conditions and Loops

Conditions and Loops is the focus of this Python for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to write understandable Python programs for safe security automation.

variable

A named reference to a stored value.

function

A reusable block of code that performs a defined task.

automation

Use of software to perform repeatable work consistently.

Conditions branch on a test: if, elif, else. Loops repeat: for iterates over a collection, while repeats until a condition changes.

Almost every log analysis script is a loop over lines with a condition inside it. Learning these two constructs well covers most of what security scripting requires.

Key points

  • if / elif / else branch on a condition.
  • for iterates over lines, lists or dictionary keys.
  • while repeats until its condition becomes false.
  • Comparison: == equals, != not equals, >, <, in.
  • Combine with and, or, not.
  • break exits a loop; continue skips to the next iteration.

Example

Reading a log file line by line, testing if "Failed password" in line, and incrementing a counter is the entire structure of a brute-force detector. Everything else is refinement.

Why this matters

This loop-and-test pattern is the skeleton of the detection workflow you build in Module 9.

lessons.title: 7.5 Functions
lessons.html:
📖 Functions
Name a piece of logic once and reuse it everywhere.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Functions

Functions is the focus of this Python for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to write understandable Python programs for safe security automation.

variable

A named reference to a stored value.

function

A reusable block of code that performs a defined task.

automation

Use of software to perform repeatable work consistently.

A function groups steps under a name, optionally takes parameters, and optionally returns a result. Defined with def, it turns repeated code into a single tested unit.

For security scripts this matters because logic that is written once is reviewed once. A parsing rule duplicated in four places will eventually be corrected in three of them.

Key points

  • def name(parameters): defines a function.
  • return sends a value back; without it, the function returns None.
  • Parameters make a function reusable across inputs.
  • Keep functions small and single-purpose — easier to test and to trust.
  • Variables inside a function are local to it.
  • Give functions verb names: parse_line, count_failures.

Example

A parse_auth_line() function used by three different scripts means a fix to the parsing rule applies everywhere at once. Duplicated inline parsing means the same fix must be found three times.

Why this matters

Small, named functions are what make a security tool maintainable by the next analyst — which is usually the point of writing it down at all.

lessons.title: 7.6 Working With Files
lessons.html:
📖 Working With Files
Reading logs and writing findings — the two ends of every analysis script.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Working With Files

Working With Files is the focus of this Python for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to write understandable Python programs for safe security automation.

variable

A named reference to a stored value.

function

A reusable block of code that performs a defined task.

automation

Use of software to perform repeatable work consistently.

Python opens files with open(), and the with statement closes them automatically even if an error occurs. Logs are read line by line rather than all at once, so a multi-gigabyte file does not exhaust memory.

For structured output, JSON and CSV are the right formats: JSON preserves structure for other tools, CSV opens in a spreadsheet for people who do not use the terminal.

Key points

  • with open(path) as f: closes the file automatically.
  • Iterate line by line for large logs rather than reading everything into memory.
  • Modes: 'r' read, 'w' overwrite, 'a' append.
  • Use 'a' for evidence logs — never overwrite collected data.
  • json and csv modules handle structured output properly.
  • Handle missing files and permission errors explicitly.

Example

Opening a 4 GB log with read() loads all of it into memory and may fail. Iterating over the file object reads one line at a time and works regardless of size.

Why this matters

Evidence handling starts here: append rather than overwrite, and record what you collected as well as what you concluded.

lessons.title: 7.7 Python and Networking

📖 Python and Networking
Talking to hosts and services from a script, safely.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Python and Networking

Python and Networking is the focus of this Python for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to write understandable Python programs for safe security automation.

variable

A named reference to a stored value.

function

A reusable block of code that performs a defined task.

automation

Use of software to perform repeatable work consistently.

Python's socket module handles raw network connections; requests handles HTTP. Between them they cover connectivity checks, banner retrieval and API calls.

In security scripting, always set a timeout. Without one a single unresponsive host hangs the whole script indefinitely, which is a common and avoidable failure.

Key points

  • socket for raw TCP/UDP; requests for HTTP and HTTPS.
  • Always set a timeout — unresponsive hosts otherwise hang the script.
  • Verify TLS certificates; never disable verification to silence an error.
  • Handle connection errors explicitly rather than letting the script crash.
  • Rate limit your own requests so you do not disrupt the target.
  • Any network interaction with a system you do not own requires authorisation.

Example

Setting verify=False to make an HTTPS error disappear silently removes the protection TLS exists to provide. The correct fix is to trust the right certificate authority, not to stop checking.

Why this matters

These habits — timeouts, error handling, certificate verification — are what separate a script that works once from one another analyst can rely on.

Most security tooling is reachable by API, and that is how you automate it.

Working With APIs

Working With APIs is the focus of this Python for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to write understandable Python programs for safe security automation.

variable

A named reference to a stored value.

function

A reusable block of code that performs a defined task.

automation

Use of software to perform repeatable work consistently.

An API lets one program ask another for data. Security platforms — threat intelligence, SIEM, ticketing, cloud providers — all expose one, usually returning JSON over HTTPS.

Handling credentials correctly is the security-critical part. API keys belong in environment variables or a secrets manager, never in the script and never in the repository.

Key points

  • Most APIs return JSON, which maps onto Python dictionaries.
  • Authenticate with a key or token, usually in a header.
  • Never hard-code credentials — use environment variables.
  • Respect rate limits; handle HTTP 429 by backing off.
  • Check the status code before parsing the response body.
  • Log what you queried, but never log the key itself.

Example

Enriching an address with a threat intelligence API turns “unknown external IP” into “known scanning infrastructure, first seen last week” automatically, for every alert, without an analyst opening a browser.

Why this matters

Enrichment is where automation pays off fastest in a SOC: the same lookup, applied consistently to every alert, before a human ever sees it.

lessons.title: 7.9 Automating Security Tasks
lessons.html:
📖 Automating Security Tasks
Automate the repetitive and the error-prone, not the judgement.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Automating Security Tasks

Automating Security Tasks is the focus of this Python for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to write understandable Python programs for safe security automation.

variable

A named reference to a stored value.

function

A reusable block of code that performs a defined task.

automation

Use of software to perform repeatable work consistently.

Good automation candidates are tasks done often, done identically each time, and prone to human slips: log parsing, enrichment, evidence collection, report formatting, configuration checks.

Poor candidates are anything requiring judgement — deciding whether an alert is a real incident, or whether to isolate a production server. Automate the gathering; leave the deciding.

Key points

  • Automate what is repetitive, identical each time, and error-prone.
  • Do not automate judgement calls, particularly disruptive actions.
  • Log what the script did, so its actions are auditable.
  • Fail safely: on error, stop and alert rather than continuing blindly.
  • Test on sample data before running against production.
  • Automation that nobody understands is a liability, not an asset.

Example

Automatically isolating any host that triggers a rule sounds efficient until a false positive isolates the payroll server on pay day. Automatic enrichment with human approval for action is the usual balance.

Why this matters

This distinction — automate collection, keep decisions human — is the same principle the AI modules apply to machine learning tools.

📖 Building a Simple Security Tool
Bringing files, loops, functions and output together.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Building a Simple Security Tool

Building a Simple Security Tool is the focus of this Python for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to write understandable Python programs for safe security automation.

variable

A named reference to a stored value.

function

A reusable block of code that performs a defined task.

automation

Use of software to perform repeatable work consistently.

A useful first tool reads an authentication log, counts failed logins per source address, and reports any address above a threshold. It combines everything in this module and produces something a SOC would actually use.

Structure it clearly: a function to parse a line, a function to analyse the collection, and a function to report. Separating those three makes each testable and lets you swap the log format without rewriting the analysis.

Key points

  • Separate parse, analyse and report into distinct functions.
  • Take the file path and threshold as arguments rather than hard-coding them.
  • Output JSON for other tools, or a readable summary for people.
  • Handle malformed lines — real logs always contain some.
  • Test against a small sample with a known answer before trusting it.
  • Document what the tool assumes about the log format.

Example

The finished tool answers a real question — “which addresses are attempting brute force against us?” — in seconds, consistently, and can be scheduled to run every morning without anyone remembering to do it.

Why this matters

This is the shape of most security tooling: parse, analyse, report. The complexity grows, but the structure does not change.

lessons.title: 8.1 AI vs. Machine Learning
lessons.html:
📖 AI vs. Machine Learning
Machine learning is the part of AI doing the work in security products.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

AI vs. Machine Learning

AI vs. Machine Learning is the focus of this Introduction to AI for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use AI tools critically and responsibly in security work.

machine learning

Methods that learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions.

model

A computational system trained or designed to produce outputs from inputs.

prompt

Instructions or context supplied to a generative AI system.

AI is the broad field. Machine learning is the subset that learns patterns from data. Deep learning is the subset of ML using layered neural networks.

Learning comes in three shapes: supervised (learning from labelled examples), unsupervised (finding structure in unlabelled data), and reinforcement (learning from feedback). Security uses the first two heavily.

Key points

  • AI → machine learning → deep learning, each a subset of the last.
  • Supervised: labelled examples — spam vs not spam, malware vs benign.
  • Unsupervised: no labels — clustering and anomaly detection.
  • Training data determines what the model can recognise.
  • Models produce probabilities, not verdicts.
  • Overfitting: a model that memorises training data and fails on new data.

Example

A malware classifier trained only on Windows samples classifies Linux binaries meaninglessly. It was never shown any, so it has nothing to compare against — the model is not wrong so much as out of scope.

Why this matters

Knowing which type of learning a tool uses tells you what it can and cannot detect, and what data it needs to stay accurate.

questions.explanation: Supervised learning trains on examples labelled with the correct answer.

lessons.title: 8.2 Generative AI
lessons.html:
📖 Generative AI
Models that produce new content rather than classify existing content.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Generative AI

Generative AI is the focus of this Introduction to AI for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use AI tools critically and responsibly in security work.

machine learning

Methods that learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions.

model

A computational system trained or designed to produce outputs from inputs.

prompt

Instructions or context supplied to a generative AI system.

Generative AI creates text, images, audio or code by predicting what plausibly comes next, based on patterns learned from very large training sets.

In security this cuts both ways. Defenders use it to summarise logs, explain alerts and draft reports. Attackers use it to write fluent phishing in any language and to generate malware variants quickly.

Key points

  • Generative models produce content; classifiers label it.
  • Output is plausible by construction, which is not the same as correct.
  • Hallucination: confidently stated content that is simply false.
  • Defensive uses: summarising, explaining, drafting, translating.
  • Offensive uses: fluent phishing at scale, malware variants, deepfakes.
  • Never paste confidential data into a public AI service.

Example

Poor grammar used to be the classic phishing signal. Generative models removed it — a fluent, correctly localised message costs an attacker nothing now, so that advice no longer works.

Why this matters

This is why Module 12 exists: the same technology that helps defenders has changed what attacks look like, and detection advice written before it needs revising.

lessons.title: 8.3 Large Language Models
lessons.html:
📖 Large Language Models
Statistical models of text, useful precisely because they are not databases.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Large Language Models

Large Language Models is the focus of this Introduction to AI for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use AI tools critically and responsibly in security work.

machine learning

Methods that learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions.

model

A computational system trained or designed to produce outputs from inputs.

prompt

Instructions or context supplied to a generative AI system.

A large language model is trained on very large volumes of text to predict the next piece of text. It has no factual database and no ability to verify — it produces what is statistically likely to follow.

That explains both its strengths and its failure mode. It summarises, rephrases and explains well. It states false specifics — a CVE number, a command flag, a log field — with exactly the same confidence as true ones.

Key points

  • An LLM predicts likely text; it does not look facts up.
  • It has a knowledge cutoff and no awareness of recent events.
  • Specific details — identifiers, versions, numbers — are the least reliable output.
  • It cannot tell you why it produced an answer.
  • The same prompt can produce different answers on different runs.
  • Always verify security-relevant output against a primary source.

Example

Asked for the CVE identifier of a vulnerability, a model may return a plausible, correctly formatted, entirely fictitious number. The format is learned; the specific value was never a fact to it.

Why this matters

This is the single most important limitation for an analyst to internalise, because an incident report containing an invented identifier damages your credibility permanently.

questions.explanation: Models know nothing about events after their training data ends.

lessons.title: 8.4 How ChatGPT and Similar AI Systems Work
lessons.html:
📖 How ChatGPT and Similar AI Systems Work
Tokens, context and probability — and why that shapes how you should use them.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

How ChatGPT and Similar AI Systems Work

How ChatGPT and Similar AI Systems Work is the focus of this Introduction to AI for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use AI tools critically and responsibly in security work.

machine learning

Methods that learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions.

model

A computational system trained or designed to produce outputs from inputs.

prompt

Instructions or context supplied to a generative AI system.

Text is broken into tokens. The model predicts the next token repeatedly, each time considering everything currently in its context window. When the context fills, the earliest content is dropped.

The model does not remember previous conversations unless that history is supplied again. Anything it appears to recall was re-sent as part of the current request.

Key points

  • Text is processed as tokens, not words.
  • The context window is the working memory for one request.
  • Output is generated one token at a time, each conditioned on what came before.
  • No memory persists between sessions unless the application re-sends it.
  • Temperature controls randomness; lower is more consistent.
  • Everything you send is processed by the provider — treat it as disclosed.

Example

Pasting 500 lines of log into a model works because they fit in the context window. Pasting 50,000 lines does not — the earliest lines fall out silently, and the answer covers only what remained.

Why this matters

Understanding the context window explains why you must chunk large inputs, and why an analyst who does not will get confidently incomplete answers.

lessons.title: 8.5 Prompt Engineering
lessons.html:
📖 Prompt Engineering
Specific instructions, real context, and a defined output format.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Prompt Engineering

Prompt Engineering is the focus of this Introduction to AI for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use AI tools critically and responsibly in security work.

machine learning

Methods that learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions.

model

A computational system trained or designed to produce outputs from inputs.

prompt

Instructions or context supplied to a generative AI system.

Prompt engineering is writing requests that produce useful, checkable answers. The reliable pattern is: state the role, give the actual data, say exactly what you want, and specify the output format.

Vague prompts produce vague answers. “Is this suspicious?” invites a guess; “here are 40 log lines, list any source address with more than five failures and quote the lines” invites a verifiable answer.

Key points

  • Be specific about the task and the output format.
  • Provide the actual data rather than describing it.
  • Ask for reasoning or evidence so the answer can be checked.
  • Break large tasks into steps rather than asking for everything at once.
  • Ask it to cite the input lines it used — then verify them.
  • Never include credentials, personal data or client information.

Example

“Analyse these 40 authentication log lines. List every source address with more than five failures, with the count and the exact lines you used.” Every part of that answer can be checked against the input.

Why this matters

Asking for evidence rather than conclusions is what makes AI assistance safe in security work: the analyst verifies rather than trusts.

lessons.title: 8.6 AI for Security Research
lessons.html:
📖 AI for Security Research
A fast way to understand unfamiliar material — then verify it.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

AI for Security Research

AI for Security Research is the focus of this Introduction to AI for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use AI tools critically and responsibly in security work.

machine learning

Methods that learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions.

model

A computational system trained or designed to produce outputs from inputs.

prompt

Instructions or context supplied to a generative AI system.

AI assistants help analysts get oriented: explaining an unfamiliar protocol, summarising a long advisory, translating a log format, or drafting a query in a syntax you use rarely.

The rule is that AI provides the starting point, never the citation. Anything that will appear in a report — a CVE number, a version range, a vendor recommendation — must be confirmed against the primary source.

Key points

  • Good uses: explaining concepts, summarising advisories, drafting queries.
  • Verify every specific fact against the vendor or the CVE record itself.
  • Never cite an AI assistant as a source in a report.
  • Ask it to explain reasoning so you can judge whether it holds up.
  • Beware confident answers about very recent events — check the cutoff.
  • Use it to learn faster, not to skip understanding.

Example

An assistant explains a vulnerability class clearly and then cites a specific CVE with the wrong affected versions. The explanation was worth having; the version range would have made the remediation advice wrong.

Why this matters

Used this way AI genuinely accelerates learning, which matters most for analysts without a mentor nearby. Used the other way it produces reports that fall apart under review.

lessons.title: 8.7 AI for Log Analysis
lessons.html:
📖 AI for Log Analysis
Turning volume into something a human can read.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

AI for Log Analysis

AI for Log Analysis is the focus of this Introduction to AI for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use AI tools critically and responsibly in security work.

machine learning

Methods that learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions.

model

A computational system trained or designed to produce outputs from inputs.

prompt

Instructions or context supplied to a generative AI system.

Logs are voluminous, repetitive and structured — which is exactly what models handle well. Useful tasks include summarising a time window, spotting outliers, correlating events across sources, and explaining an unfamiliar log format.

The discipline is to keep the model inside the data you gave it. Ask it to quote the lines supporting each observation, then check those lines yourself before acting.

Key points

  • Effective tasks: summarise, cluster, correlate, explain unfamiliar formats.
  • Always require the supporting log lines to be quoted.
  • Chunk large logs — the context window is finite and truncation is silent.
  • Redact usernames, addresses and hostnames when using an external service.
  • The model does not know your environment's normal — you supply that context.
  • Confirm every finding in the original log before it enters a report.

Example

Asked to summarise 300 lines and quote its evidence, a model highlights one account authenticating from two countries within minutes and quotes both lines. The analyst reads those two lines and confirms it in seconds.

Why this matters

This is the highest-value everyday use of AI in a SOC, and the quote-your-evidence habit is what makes it safe.

lessons.title: 8.8 AI for Threat Detection
lessons.html:
📖 AI for Threat Detection
Models that flag the unusual, and the arithmetic of false positives.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

AI for Threat Detection

AI for Threat Detection is the focus of this Introduction to AI for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use AI tools critically and responsibly in security work.

machine learning

Methods that learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions.

model

A computational system trained or designed to produce outputs from inputs.

prompt

Instructions or context supplied to a generative AI system.

Detection models learn a baseline of normal behaviour and flag departures from it. They catch things signatures miss, including activity nobody has catalogued.

The hard part is base rates. On a network with millions of daily events, even a very accurate model produces large numbers of false positives simply because almost everything is benign.

Key points

  • Models detect novel behaviour that signature rules cannot describe.
  • A baseline period is required, and it must be free of active compromise.
  • False positive: benign flagged as malicious. False negative: attack missed.
  • At low base rates, even 99% accuracy yields many false positives.
  • Tuning trades sensitivity against analyst workload.
  • Models drift as the environment changes; they need retraining.

Example

A model that is 99% accurate, run over a million daily events of which 100 are malicious, produces around 10,000 false positives. The accuracy figure was never the useful number — precision at the alerting threshold is.

Why this matters

This arithmetic explains why tuning consumes so much of a detection engineer's time, and why vendor accuracy claims mean little without the base rate.

lessons.title: 8.9 AI-Assisted Security Automation
lessons.html:
📖 AI-Assisted Security Automation
Let the machine gather; let the human decide.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

AI-Assisted Security Automation

AI-Assisted Security Automation is the focus of this Introduction to AI for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use AI tools critically and responsibly in security work.

machine learning

Methods that learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions.

model

A computational system trained or designed to produce outputs from inputs.

prompt

Instructions or context supplied to a generative AI system.

AI fits naturally into the gathering and summarising parts of a workflow: enriching alerts, drafting queries, correlating sources, producing first-draft documentation.

It fits badly into decisions with consequences. Automated containment based on a model's output will eventually isolate something critical on the basis of a false positive, which is why approval gates exist.

Key points

  • Automate enrichment, correlation and drafting.
  • Keep a human approval step before disruptive actions.
  • Log every automated action for audit and rollback.
  • Define the blast radius before enabling any automatic response.
  • Test automation against historical incidents before trusting it live.
  • Review automated decisions periodically — drift affects them too.

Example

Automatically enriching every alert with threat intelligence and asset ownership saves each analyst hours a week and carries no risk. Automatically isolating hosts on the same signal carries a great deal.

Why this matters

The division — automate collection, gate action — is the same conclusion Module 7 reached for scripting, and it holds for AI for the same reason.

lessons.title: 8.10 Limitations of AI in Cybersecurity
lessons.html:
📖 Limitations of AI in Cybersecurity
Knowing where it fails is what makes it usable.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Limitations of AI in Cybersecurity

Limitations of AI in Cybersecurity is the focus of this Introduction to AI for Cybersecurity lesson. It develops the learner's ability to use AI tools critically and responsibly in security work.

machine learning

Methods that learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions.

model

A computational system trained or designed to produce outputs from inputs.

prompt

Instructions or context supplied to a generative AI system.

AI models are only as good as their training data, they cannot explain themselves clearly, they degrade as environments change, and they can be deliberately manipulated by an attacker who understands them.

They also cannot supply context. A model does not know that this server is decommissioned, that this contractor's access was approved yesterday, or that this transfer is routine for this department.

Key points

  • Output quality is bounded by training data quality and coverage.
  • Many models cannot explain why they flagged something.
  • Drift: accuracy falls as environments and attacks change.
  • Adversarial input can be crafted to evade or mislead a model.
  • Models lack organisational context that analysts hold.
  • Over-trusting AI output is itself a security risk.

Example

A model flags a large overnight data transfer as exfiltration. The analyst knows it is the scheduled monthly backup to the disaster recovery site. The model had no way to know that, and never will unless it is told.

Why this matters

Every limitation here becomes an attack in Module 12. Understanding them is what stops AI tooling from becoming a false sense of security.

lessons.title: 9.1 Understanding Security Logs
lessons.html:
📖 Understanding Security Logs
Logs are the evidence; reading them is the core analyst skill.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Understanding Security Logs

Understanding Security Logs is the focus of this AI-Powered Threat Detection lesson. It develops the learner's ability to identify suspicious patterns while validating AI-generated alerts.

anomaly

An observation that differs meaningfully from expected behavior.

indicator of compromise

Observable evidence suggesting a security incident.

false positive

A benign event incorrectly identified as malicious.

Every system records what happened: authentication attempts, network connections, process starts, file access, web requests. An analyst's job begins with knowing which log answers which question.

Two things make logs usable: accurate time synchronised across systems, and retention long enough to investigate. Without both, correlation is impossible and incidents cannot be reconstructed.

Key points

  • Common sources: authentication, firewall, DNS, proxy, endpoint, application.
  • NTP time sync is essential — correlation depends on it.
  • Record time zones explicitly; prefer UTC in analysis.
  • Retention must exceed typical detection delay, often months.
  • Ship logs off-host so an attacker cannot erase them.
  • A log entry records what was observed, not necessarily what was intended.

Example

Two systems whose clocks differ by three minutes make a login and the connection it caused appear in the wrong order. The analyst reconstructs a sequence that never happened — from entirely accurate logs.

Why this matters

Everything in Modules 9, 10 and 11 depends on logs being complete, time-accurate and preserved. Those three properties are worth more than any detection tool.

lessons.title: 9.2 Identifying Suspicious Activity
lessons.html:
📖 Identifying Suspicious Activity
Suspicion is a comparison against normal, so learn normal first.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Identifying Suspicious Activity

Identifying Suspicious Activity is the focus of this AI-Powered Threat Detection lesson. It develops the learner's ability to identify suspicious patterns while validating AI-generated alerts.

anomaly

An observation that differs meaningfully from expected behavior.

indicator of compromise

Observable evidence suggesting a security incident.

false positive

A benign event incorrectly identified as malicious.

Nothing is suspicious in isolation. A login at 3am is unremarkable for a night-shift engineer and significant for an accounts clerk. Detection is always a comparison against an established baseline.

The recurring signals are timing, volume, location, sequence and privilege: activity at unusual hours, unusual data volumes, unexpected locations, actions in an implausible order, or a sudden change in what an account does.

Key points

  • Establish normal before deciding what is abnormal.
  • Timing: activity outside the account's usual pattern.
  • Volume: transfers or request rates far above baseline.
  • Location: impossible travel, or unexpected countries.
  • Sequence: events in an order that should not occur.
  • Privilege: a normal account suddenly performing administrative actions.

Example

A service account that has only ever authenticated from one server begins authenticating interactively from a workstation. Nothing failed and nothing was blocked — the change in pattern is the entire signal.

Why this matters

This is the analytical habit the whole job rests on: not “is this bad?” but “is this different, and can it be explained?”

lessons.title: 9.3 Detecting Anomalies
lessons.html:
📖 Detecting Anomalies
Statistical and behavioural methods for finding what rules cannot describe.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Detecting Anomalies

Detecting Anomalies is the focus of this AI-Powered Threat Detection lesson. It develops the learner's ability to identify suspicious patterns while validating AI-generated alerts.

anomaly

An observation that differs meaningfully from expected behavior.

indicator of compromise

Observable evidence suggesting a security incident.

false positive

A benign event incorrectly identified as malicious.

Anomaly detection establishes a baseline mathematically and flags departures. It catches what nobody wrote a rule for — which is its whole value and the source of its false positives.

The baseline period must be free of compromise. If an attacker was already present while the baseline was learned, their activity becomes part of “normal” and will never be flagged.

Key points

  • Baselines can be per-user, per-host, per-service or organisation-wide.
  • A compromised baseline period teaches the model that the attack is normal.
  • Seasonal patterns matter: month-end and pay day are legitimately different.
  • Anomalous is not malicious — it means unexplained.
  • Combine anomaly detection with rules; each catches what the other misses.
  • Tune to your environment; vendor defaults rarely fit.

Example

A finance system's transaction volume triples at month-end every month. A model baselined on mid-month data flags it as anomalous every time, and analysts learn to ignore that alert — including the month something is genuinely wrong.

Why this matters

An alert people learn to ignore is worse than no alert, which is why tuning is a continuous task rather than a deployment step.

lessons.title: 9.4 AI-Based Malware Detection
lessons.html:
📖 AI-Based Malware Detection
Classifying files and behaviour by similarity rather than exact match.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

AI-Based Malware Detection

AI-Based Malware Detection is the focus of this AI-Powered Threat Detection lesson. It develops the learner's ability to identify suspicious patterns while validating AI-generated alerts.

anomaly

An observation that differs meaningfully from expected behavior.

indicator of compromise

Observable evidence suggesting a security incident.

false positive

A benign event incorrectly identified as malicious.

Signature detection matches known samples exactly. Machine learning classifies by features — file structure, imported functions, entropy, runtime behaviour — so it can flag variants never seen before.

Static analysis examines a file without running it. Dynamic analysis runs it in a sandbox and observes behaviour. Modern tooling combines both, because each has evasions the other catches.

Key points

  • Signatures catch known samples; ML classifies unseen variants by similarity.
  • Static: examine the file. Dynamic: run it in a sandbox.
  • High entropy suggests packing or encryption — suspicious, not conclusive.
  • Malware may detect a sandbox and behave benignly inside it.
  • Behavioural detection catches fileless attacks that leave no file.
  • Never execute suspected malware outside an isolated analysis environment.

Example

A packed executable shows high entropy and imports functions associated with process injection. Neither proves malice — legitimate packers exist — but together they justify sandbox analysis before the file is allowed to run.

Why this matters

This feeds Module 11's malware incident response, where the classification decides how the incident is handled.

lessons.title: 9.5 Phishing Detection With AI

📖 Phishing Detection With AI
Scoring many weak signals at once, because no single one is decisive.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Phishing Detection With AI

Phishing Detection With AI is the focus of this AI-Powered Threat Detection lesson. It develops the learner's ability to identify suspicious patterns while validating AI-generated alerts.

anomaly

An observation that differs meaningfully from expected behavior.

indicator of compromise

Observable evidence suggesting a security incident.

false positive

A benign event incorrectly identified as malicious.

Phishing detection models weigh sender reputation, domain age, header consistency, link structure, urgency language and similarity to known campaigns. No single feature decides; the combination does.

Generative AI removed the easiest signal by producing fluent text, so detection has shifted further toward technical indicators: authentication results, domain registration age, and link destinations.

Key points

  • Signals: sender reputation, SPF/DKIM/DMARC results, domain age, link structure.
  • Language cues remain useful but are much weaker than they were.
  • Look-alike domains substitute similar characters or add words.
  • A newly registered domain in a business email is a strong signal.
  • Check where a link actually goes, not what its text claims.
  • User reporting remains one of the most valuable detection channels.

Example

An email passes SPF, reads perfectly, and comes from a domain registered eleven days ago that differs from the real one by a single character. Two technical signals identify it; the language gives nothing away.

Why this matters

Phishing remains the most common initial access method, so this is among the highest-value detection capabilities an organisation can have.

lessons.title: 9.6 Threat Intelligence
lessons.html:
📖 Threat Intelligence
Knowing what others have already seen, so you do not learn it the hard way.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Threat Intelligence

Threat Intelligence is the focus of this AI-Powered Threat Detection lesson. It develops the learner's ability to identify suspicious patterns while validating AI-generated alerts.

anomaly

An observation that differs meaningfully from expected behavior.

indicator of compromise

Observable evidence suggesting a security incident.

false positive

A benign event incorrectly identified as malicious.

Threat intelligence is information about adversaries: their infrastructure, tools, techniques and current campaigns. It ranges from simple indicator feeds to detailed analysis of a group's behaviour.

The most durable form describes behaviour rather than artefacts. An attacker changes an IP address in minutes; changing how they establish persistence takes far longer.

Key points

  • Tactical: indicators — addresses, hashes, domains. Perishable.
  • Operational: campaigns and techniques currently in use.
  • Strategic: who targets your sector, and why.
  • Behaviour-based intelligence outlasts indicator-based intelligence.
  • MITRE ATT&CK is the common vocabulary for adversary techniques.
  • Relevance matters: intelligence about a sector you are not in is noise.

Example

Blocking a list of malicious IP addresses helps for days. Detecting the technique — say, persistence through a scheduled task — keeps working after the attacker rebuilds their infrastructure.

Why this matters

This is why ATT&CK became the industry's shared reference: it describes what attackers do, which changes far more slowly than what they use.

lessons.title: 9.7 Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)
