lessons.title: 13.10 Cloud Security Best Practices
lessons.html:
📖 Cloud Security Best Practices
A checklist that addresses most of what actually goes wrong.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Cloud Security Best Practices

Cloud Security Best Practices is the focus of this Cloud and AI Security lesson. It develops the learner's ability to protect identities, data, networks, applications, and AI services in cloud environments.

cloud computing

On-demand delivery of computing resources over a network.

identity and access management

Policies and tools controlling digital identities and permissions.

shared responsibility

Division of security duties between a cloud provider and customer.

Consolidating the module: control identity tightly, log everything, restrict network exposure, protect data, monitor configuration continuously, and know what you own.

Apply these consistently rather than perfectly. Most cloud breaches happen in the one account, the one project or the one resource that the standard was never applied to.

Key points

  • Enforce MFA everywhere; never use root or owner accounts routinely.
  • Apply least privilege and review permissions on a schedule.
  • Enable audit logging in every account, shipped to a separate one.
  • Default deny on network rules; no management ports facing the internet.
  • Encrypt data, manage keys deliberately, and check for public storage daily.
  • Tag every resource with an owner and review orphans regularly.

Example

Applying this checklist to nine of ten accounts leaves the tenth as the entry point. Consistency across the whole estate matters more than depth in part of it.

Why this matters

This is the closing practical summary of the technical course, and it is the standard against which the Module 14 projects are assessed.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Security Assessment Project
lessons.html:
📖 Security Assessment Project
Assess a system you own, and write the report an employer would read.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Security Assessment Project

Security Assessment Project is the focus of this Real-World Cybersecurity Projects lesson. It develops the learner's ability to combine course skills in an authorized, documented defensive project.

project scope

The approved goals, systems, methods, and limits of a project.

deliverable

A completed product or report produced by a project.

validation

Evidence-based confirmation that a result meets requirements.

Build a target in your own lab — a virtual machine running a web application and a couple of services — and assess it end to end: enumerate the attack surface, identify weaknesses, verify them, and report.

The deliverable is the report, not the findings. Follow the structure from Module 5: executive summary, findings with evidence and reproduction steps, business impact, and specific remediation.

Key points

  • Target must be your own lab VM. Nothing else is authorised.
  • Enumerate: hosts, open ports, services, versions, exposed applications.
  • Verify every finding — do not report unvalidated scanner output.
  • Write findings as: description, location, evidence, impact, remediation.
  • Rate by business risk, not scanner severity alone.
  • Include an executive summary in non-technical language.

Example

Suggested target: an intentionally vulnerable web application VM, plus a Linux host with SSH and a web server. Expect to find default credentials, missing patches, over-permissive file permissions and at least one web flaw from Module 6.

Why this matters

This is the portfolio piece that demonstrates you can do the work and communicate it. A clear five-page report is worth more in an interview than a long list of tool output.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Phishing Detection Project
lessons.html:
📖 Phishing Detection Project
Build a scoring tool that explains its reasoning.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Phishing Detection Project

Phishing Detection Project is the focus of this Real-World Cybersecurity Projects lesson. It develops the learner's ability to combine course skills in an authorized, documented defensive project.

project scope

The approved goals, systems, methods, and limits of a project.

deliverable

A completed product or report produced by a project.

validation

Evidence-based confirmation that a result meets requirements.

Write a Python tool that takes an email (headers and body) and produces a risk score with the reasons behind it. Use the signals from Module 9: authentication results, sender domain age, link destinations, look-alike domains and language cues.

The requirement that matters is explainability. A score alone is not usable by an analyst; a score with the three signals that produced it is.

Key points

  • Input: a saved email file. Output: a score plus the reasons for it.
  • Signals: SPF/DKIM/DMARC results, domain age, link destination, look-alike domain.
  • Compare displayed link text against the actual destination.
  • Explain every point contributed to the score.
  • Test against both phishing samples and legitimate mail.
  • Report your false positive rate honestly.

Example

Use safely obtained samples — your own spam folder, or a public phishing corpus. Never open links or attachments from real phishing samples outside an isolated VM.

Why this matters

Explainable output is the difference between a tool a SOC would adopt and one that produces numbers nobody trusts. Measuring your own false positive rate shows you understand the arithmetic from Module 9.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Log Analysis Project
lessons.html:
📖 Log Analysis Project
Turn a raw log into a defensible finding.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Log Analysis Project

Log Analysis Project is the focus of this Real-World Cybersecurity Projects lesson. It develops the learner's ability to combine course skills in an authorized, documented defensive project.

project scope

The approved goals, systems, methods, and limits of a project.

deliverable

A completed product or report produced by a project.

validation

Evidence-based confirmation that a result meets requirements.

Take an authentication log — from your own lab, or a public sample dataset — and build an analysis that identifies brute-force attempts, unusual login times and impossible travel.

Produce two outputs: a machine-readable JSON summary and a short written finding that states what you observed, which lines support it, and what you recommend.

Key points

  • Parse the log into structured records with a dedicated function.
  • Detect: repeated failures per source, off-hours logins, impossible travel.
  • Handle malformed lines without crashing.
  • Output JSON for tooling and a written summary for people.
  • Quote the specific log lines supporting each finding.
  • State your thresholds and justify them.

Example

Suggested threshold to start: more than ten failures from one source within five minutes. Then examine what that threshold misses and what it falsely flags, and adjust with your reasoning recorded.

Why this matters

Justifying a threshold, and knowing what it misses, is exactly the detection-engineering reasoning from Module 9. That reasoning is what makes the project worth showing.

lessons.title: 🛠️ AI Security Assistant Project
lessons.html:
📖 AI Security Assistant Project
Use an AI assistant safely inside a defined workflow.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

AI Security Assistant Project

AI Security Assistant Project is the focus of this Real-World Cybersecurity Projects lesson. It develops the learner's ability to combine course skills in an authorized, documented defensive project.

project scope

The approved goals, systems, methods, and limits of a project.

deliverable

A completed product or report produced by a project.

validation

Evidence-based confirmation that a result meets requirements.

Build a small workflow where an AI assistant helps analyse security data — summarising logs, explaining an alert, or drafting an incident note — with the safeguards from Modules 8 and 12 applied.

The safeguards are the assessed part: redact sensitive data before sending, require the model to quote its evidence, verify that evidence against the source, and never let model output trigger an action directly.

Key points

  • Define the task narrowly — summarise, explain, or draft.
  • Redact usernames, hostnames and addresses before sending.
  • Require the model to quote the input lines supporting each statement.
  • Verify every quoted line against the original data.
  • Never let output trigger an action without human approval.
  • Document at least one case where the model was wrong.

Example

Documenting a failure is a requirement, not an embarrassment. Every model produces confident errors, and showing you detected one demonstrates the verification discipline the whole AI section teaches.

Why this matters

This project demonstrates the judgement employers are most concerned about with AI-assisted analysts: that you verify rather than trust.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Incident Response Project
lessons.html:
📖 Incident Response Project
Run a simulated incident from detection to report.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Incident Response Project

Incident Response Project is the focus of this Real-World Cybersecurity Projects lesson. It develops the learner's ability to combine course skills in an authorized, documented defensive project.

project scope

The approved goals, systems, methods, and limits of a project.

deliverable

A completed product or report produced by a project.

validation

Evidence-based confirmation that a result meets requirements.

Simulate an incident in your lab: a phishing click leading to credential use, or a suspicious process establishing persistence. Then respond to it properly — detect, contain, investigate, eradicate, recover, report.

Build the timeline from evidence rather than from what you know you did. Working only from the artefacts is what makes the exercise realistic.

Key points

  • Simulate the incident yourself so you know the ground truth.
  • Investigate from the evidence only, not from memory.
  • Preserve volatile evidence before containment where possible.
  • Build a timeline with absolute, timezone-qualified timestamps.
  • Establish scope before remediating.
  • Write the report: summary, timeline, impact, actions, root cause, recommendations.

Example

Compare your reconstructed timeline against what you actually did. The gaps show exactly which logs you were not collecting — which is itself one of the most valuable findings the exercise produces.

Why this matters

That comparison is the whole point: it converts an exercise into a concrete list of visibility gaps, which is what a real lessons-learned review delivers.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Final Capstone Project
lessons.html:
📖 Final Capstone Project
Everything together, on one scenario, documented for a portfolio.

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Final Capstone Project

Final Capstone Project is the focus of this Real-World Cybersecurity Projects lesson. It develops the learner's ability to combine course skills in an authorized, documented defensive project.

project scope

The approved goals, systems, methods, and limits of a project.

deliverable

A completed product or report produced by a project.

validation

Evidence-based confirmation that a result meets requirements.

Choose a realistic scenario for a small organisation — a clinic, a school, a microfinance office — and produce a complete piece of security work: assess the environment, design controls, build one detection, and document an incident response plan.

Scope it to what you can genuinely complete and evidence. A narrow, finished, well-documented capstone is worth considerably more than a broad, half-built one.

Key points

  • Define the organisation, its data, and its realistic threats.
  • Assess the current state against the controls from Modules 3, 10 and 13.
  • Recommend prioritised controls with justification and rough cost.
  • Build and demonstrate at least one working detection.
  • Write an incident response plan appropriate to the organisation's size.
  • Present it as a portfolio document, not as notes.

Example

Ground it locally: a Monrovia clinic holding patient records, using cloud email and a shared internet connection, with no dedicated IT staff. Realistic constraints produce realistic and defensible recommendations.

Why this matters

This is the piece to put in front of an employer. It shows you can assess, prioritise, build and communicate — which is the whole job, and more than any certificate demonstrates on its own.

questions.question: Why should analysis be performed on a copy rather than the original?
options: Working on the original alters evidence such as timestamps
questions.explanation: Any interaction with the original risks changing the metadata the investigation depends on.

questions.question: Why is 'poor grammar' now a misleading phishing indicator?
options: Generative AI produces fluent text in any language at no cost
questions.explanation: Language quality no longer distinguishes fraudulent messages from legitimate ones.

questions.question: Under shared responsibility, who secures customer data and configuration?
questions.explanation: Providers secure the underlying infrastructure; configuration, identity and data remain the customer's responsibility.

questions.question: What are the three goals of the CIA triad?
questions.explanation: The CIA triad is confidentiality, integrity and availability, the three goals security exists to protect.

questions.question: What is privilege escalation?
options: Gaining higher permissions than the account was granted
questions.explanation: Privilege escalation moves an attacker from a limited account to administrative control.

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication proves identity; authorization decides permitted actions
questions.explanation: Identity is established first, then permissions are evaluated for that identity.

lessons.title: 📝 Linux Assessment
lessons.html:
Module 15: Final Assessment & GraduationAssessment

Linux Assessment

Complete this assessment, then review every answer explanation to strengthen weak areas.

questions.question: Why should security practice happen inside a virtual machine?
options: It isolates experiments from your real system and can be restored
questions.explanation: A VM gives an isolated, disposable environment that can be rolled back to a snapshot.

questions.question: Is good intent a legal defence for unauthorised scanning?
options: No, unauthorised access remains an offence regardless of intent
questions.explanation: Most computer-misuse laws turn on authorisation, not on the tester's motive.

questions.question: What does HTTPS add to HTTP?
options: Encryption in transit and authentication of the server's domain
questions.explanation: TLS encrypts the connection and verifies that you are talking to the named domain.

questions.question: Why use a Python virtual environment?
options: It isolates each project's dependencies from the system and other projects
questions.explanation: Isolation prevents one project's packages from breaking another or the system Python.

questions.question: What does 'hallucination' mean in generative AI?
options: It produces confident content that is factually false
questions.explanation: Generative models optimise for plausibility, so fluent but incorrect output is a normal failure mode.

questions.question: Why can no single event be suspicious in isolation?
options: Suspicion is a comparison against what is normal for that context
questions.explanation: The same action can be routine in one context and significant in another.

questions.question: In what order should an alert queue be worked?
questions.explanation: Priority ordering ensures the most consequential alerts get attention first.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a write blocker?
options: To prevent the acquisition process from modifying the source media
questions.explanation: It guarantees the evidence drive is only read, never written to.

lessons.title: 📝 Ethical Hacking Assessment
lessons.html:
Module 15: Final Assessment & GraduationAssessment

Ethical Hacking Assessment

Complete this assessment, then review every answer explanation to strengthen weak areas.

questions.question: How much audio is typically needed to clone a voice convincingly?
questions.explanation: Modern voice cloning requires only a very short sample of recorded speech.

questions.question: Why is identity described as the cloud perimeter?
options: Networks do not exist in cloud
Access is controlled by credentials rather than network position
questions.explanation: Without a network edge, possession of valid credentials is what grants access.

questions.question: Why is AI increasingly necessary in cybersecurity?
options: It is cheaper than software licences
Event volume far exceeds what human analysts can review
It removes the need for firewalls
questions.explanation: Organisations generate far more security events than any team can read, so automated triage is essential.

questions.question: What does 'persistence' mean in an attack?
options: The malicious code survives a reboot
The attacker keeps trying to log in
questions.explanation: Persistence mechanisms such as services and scheduled tasks restart malicious code after a restart.

questions.question: What contributes most to password strength?
questions.explanation: Long, unpredictable passphrases resist guessing far better than short substituted strings.

questions.question: Which command searches for text inside files?
questions.explanation: grep searches file contents for a pattern and is the core tool of log analysis.

questions.question: What distinguishes passive from active reconnaissance?
options: Passive uses public sources without touching the target
questions.explanation: Passive gathering never interacts with the target, so it leaves no trace on their systems.

questions.question: What does the HttpOnly cookie flag do?
options: Prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie
questions.explanation: HttpOnly blocks script access, which limits cookie theft through cross-site scripting.

lessons.title: 📝 Python Assessment
lessons.html:
Module 15: Final Assessment & GraduationAssessment

Python Assessment

Complete this assessment, then review every answer explanation to strengthen weak areas.

questions.question: Which structure best counts events per IP address?
options: A dictionary mapping address to count
questions.explanation: Dictionaries map a key to a value, which is exactly the shape of a per-address count.

questions.question: How does a large language model produce its answers?
questions.explanation: LLMs generate text based on learned statistical patterns, not by looking facts up.

questions.question: What happens if the baseline period contains an active compromise?
options: The attacker's activity is learned as normal and will not be flagged
questions.explanation: Baselines define normal, so anything present during baselining becomes normal.

questions.question: What determines a SIEM's detection coverage?
options: Which log sources are actually being collected
questions.explanation: No rule can detect activity in a log source that is not being ingested.

questions.question: What does chain of custody record?
options: Every person who handled the evidence, when and why
questions.explanation: An unbroken handling record is what demonstrates the evidence was not altered.

questions.question: What has AI changed about social engineering?
options: The cost of researching and personalising attacks at scale
questions.explanation: The manipulation techniques are unchanged; automation made convincing personalisation cheap.

questions.question: Why should workloads use roles rather than long-lived access keys?
options: Roles provide short-lived credentials that cannot be stolen and reused indefinitely
questions.explanation: Temporary credentials expire, limiting the value of a leaked secret.

questions.question: What does ransomware do?
options: Encrypts data and demands payment for its return
questions.explanation: Ransomware encrypts an organisation's data and demands payment in exchange for decryption.

lessons.title: 📝 AI Security Assessment
lessons.html:
Module 15: Final Assessment & GraduationAssessment

AI Security Assessment

Complete this assessment, then review every answer explanation to strengthen weak areas.

questions.question: What is lateral movement?
options: Moving a server to another rack
An attacker spreading from one compromised machine to others
questions.explanation: Lateral movement is how a single compromised host becomes a network-wide incident.

questions.question: Which combination is genuine multi-factor authentication?
options: A password and a code from an authenticator app
A password and a security question
questions.explanation: MFA requires factors from different categories; a password and a device-generated code qualify.

questions.question: Which directory holds Linux system logs?
questions.explanation: /var/log contains system and application logs, the primary evidence source on Linux.

questions.question: What is the most common serious finding when mapping attack surface?
options: Forgotten assets nobody knew were still exposed
questions.explanation: Systems that everyone stopped maintaining but nobody switched off are a recurring source of breaches.

questions.question: Why should login errors be identical for wrong username and wrong password?
options: Different messages let an attacker enumerate valid accounts
questions.explanation: Distinct messages confirm which accounts exist, narrowing an attacker's target list.

questions.question: Which loop iterates over each line of a file?
questions.explanation: A for loop iterates over a collection, including the lines of an open file.

questions.question: What is a context window?
options: The amount of text the model can consider in one request
questions.explanation: The context window bounds how much input and output the model can handle at once.

questions.question: What is the advantage of ML-based malware detection over signatures?
options: It can classify variants that have never been seen before
questions.explanation: Feature-based classification generalises to new samples, which exact signature matching cannot.

lessons.title: 📝 Threat Detection Assessment
lessons.html:
Module 15: Final Assessment & GraduationAssessment

Threat Detection Assessment

Complete this assessment, then review every answer explanation to strengthen weak areas.

questions.question: Why should the SOC alert on a log source going silent?
options: Because absence of events produces no alert and hides a collection failure
questions.explanation: A stopped source fails silently, leaving a blind spot nobody notices.

questions.question: Why are deleted files often recoverable?
options: Deletion usually marks the space reusable rather than erasing the contents
questions.explanation: Until the space is overwritten, the original data typically remains on the media.

questions.question: What is a poisoning attack?
options: Corrupting training data so the model learns incorrect behaviour
questions.explanation: Poisoning targets the training phase so the deployed model behaves wrongly by design.

questions.question: What causes the classic cloud data breach?
questions.explanation: Publicly accessible storage is a configuration mistake, not an exploited vulnerability.

questions.question: Which role is the most common entry point into cybersecurity?
questions.explanation: Tier 1 SOC analysis, monitoring and triaging alerts, is the standard entry-level defensive role.

questions.question: Which of these is a private IP address range?
questions.explanation: 192.168.x.x is one of the reserved private ranges, not routable across the internet.

questions.question: What is the key difference between hashing and encryption?
options: Hashing is one-way and cannot be reversed
questions.explanation: Encryption is reversible with a key; hashing is a one-way function used to verify integrity.

questions.question: What does permission 755 grant?
options: rwx for owner, r-x for group and others
questions.explanation: 7 is rwx for the owner, and 5 is r-x for group and others.

lessons.title: 📝 Incident Response Assessment
lessons.html:
Module 15: Final Assessment & GraduationAssessment

Incident Response Assessment

Complete this assessment, then review every answer explanation to strengthen weak areas.

questions.question: What does a CVE identifier represent?
questions.explanation: CVE is the catalogue identifier for a particular known vulnerability; CVSS scores its severity.

questions.question: What is an insecure direct object reference?
options: Accessing another user's record by changing an identifier, with no ownership check
questions.explanation: The application confirms authentication but not that the requested object belongs to that user.

questions.question: What does a function return if it has no return statement?
questions.explanation: A function without an explicit return produces None.

questions.question: What makes a prompt produce a checkable answer?
options: Providing the data and asking for the evidence used
questions.explanation: Requiring the model to cite the input it relied on lets the analyst verify the result.

questions.question: Why has language quality become a weak phishing signal?
options: Generative AI produces fluent text in any language at no cost
questions.explanation: Fluent, well-localised phishing is now trivially cheap to produce.

questions.question: What is the primary risk of high alert volume?
options: Alert fatigue causing superficial triage and missed incidents
questions.explanation: When volume exceeds capacity, genuine detections are dismissed alongside noise.

questions.question: Where are Linux authentication events typically recorded?
questions.explanation: Authentication events are written to auth.log or the systemd journal.

questions.question: Why is prompt injection possible?
options: Models cannot reliably distinguish instructions from data
questions.explanation: Instructions and content arrive through the same channel, so content can act as instruction.

lessons.title: 🧪 Final Practical Examination
lessons.html:
Module 15: Final Assessment & GraduationAssessment

Final Practical Examination

Complete this practical examination, then review every answer explanation to strengthen weak areas.

questions.question: What is the most common serious cloud network finding?
options: Management ports such as SSH or RDP open to the internet
questions.explanation: Broad access rules added during troubleshooting and left in place are a recurring cause of compromise.

questions.question: What is anomaly detection?
options: Flagging behaviour that differs from an established baseline
questions.explanation: Anomaly detection learns what normal looks like and highlights departures from it.

questions.question: At which level does a MAC address operate?
options: Within the local network segment only
questions.explanation: MAC addresses are link-layer identifiers and are not forwarded across routers.

questions.question: What does a 'default deny' firewall policy mean?
options: Block everything, then permit only what is required
questions.explanation: Default deny fails safe: anything not explicitly permitted, including novel traffic, is blocked.

questions.question: Which command shows which process is listening on which port?
questions.explanation: ss -tulpn lists listening sockets together with the owning process.

questions.question: What does a port scan reveal?
options: Which services are listening on a host
questions.explanation: Port scanning identifies open ports and, with service detection, what is running behind them.

questions.question: What is the correct defence against SQL injection?
options: Parameterised queries that separate structure from data
questions.explanation: Parameterisation means user input can never be interpreted as query structure.

questions.question: Why use 'with open(...)' rather than a bare open()?
options: The file is closed automatically, even if an error occurs
questions.explanation: The context manager guarantees the file handle is released.

questions.question: How should AI-provided facts be treated before use in a report?
questions.explanation: Specifics such as identifiers and version ranges must be confirmed with the vendor or CVE record.

questions.question: Which form of threat intelligence has the longest useful life?
questions.explanation: Infrastructure changes quickly; the techniques attackers rely on change slowly.

questions.question: What are the three possible outcomes of alert triage?
options: Benign with reasoning, investigate further, or declare an incident
questions.explanation: Triage routes each alert to one of these three documented outcomes.

questions.question: What is the central artefact of an incident investigation?
options: A timeline of events across systems
questions.explanation: An ordered account of events is what answers scope and causation questions.

questions.question: What happens to data sent to a third-party AI service?
options: It is processed on their infrastructure and may be retained or logged
It is always encrypted end to end
questions.explanation: Submission is a disclosure to the provider, governed by their terms.

questions.question: Where should application credentials be stored in cloud?
options: In environment files in the repository
questions.explanation: Managed secrets services provide controlled, auditable, rotatable credential storage.

questions.question: What does an AI security model actually output?
options: An exact copy of the input
questions.explanation: Models produce likelihoods, which is why human review of AI security findings remains necessary.

questions.question: What does DNS do?
options: Resolves domain names into IP addresses
questions.explanation: DNS translates human-readable names into the IP addresses machines use.

questions.question: What is the main limitation of signature-based antivirus?
options: It detects only malware that has already been catalogued
questions.explanation: Signatures match known samples, so novel or modified malware passes undetected.

questions.question: Why are repository packages safer than downloaded binaries?
options: They are cryptographically signed and verified on install
questions.explanation: Signature verification confirms the package came from the distribution and was not altered.

questions.question: What is the most common root cause of exploited vulnerabilities?
questions.explanation: Most successful exploitation targets vulnerabilities for which a patch was already available.

questions.question: Which form of XSS affects every visitor to a page?
questions.explanation: Stored XSS is saved server-side and served to everyone who views the affected page.

lessons.title: 15.1 Certificate Requirements
lessons.html:
📖 Certificate Requirements
What you must complete to graduate from this programme.

The certificate records completion of the full programme: the technical modules, the six real-world projects, the skill assessments and the final graduation assessment.

Lessons unlock in order, so the requirements are met by working through the course as designed. Retakes are unlimited, so a failed assessment costs time rather than progress.

Key points

  • Complete all lessons in Modules 1–13.
  • Complete the six projects in Module 14.
  • Pass the module skill assessments and the Final Practical Examination.
  • Pass the Graduation Assessment with 70% or higher.
  • Retakes are unlimited.
  • All practical work must be legal, ethical and confined to systems you own or are authorised to test.

Example

The certificate appears in the course player automatically once every requirement is met. Keep your six project write-ups — they are the portfolio evidence an employer will actually ask to see.

Why this matters

For an entry-level SOC application, a portfolio of six documented projects demonstrates more than the certificate alone, which is why the projects are a graduation requirement rather than an optional extra.

Certificate of Completion

questions.question: Why must network scripts set a timeout?
options: Without one, an unresponsive host hangs the script indefinitely
It is required by the socket module
questions.explanation: A missing timeout means a single silent host can stall the entire run.

questions.question: What should you always require when using AI for log analysis?
options: The specific log lines supporting each observation
questions.explanation: Quoted evidence lets the analyst verify the finding against the original log.

questions.question: Why are file hashes considered weak indicators?
options: Changing a single byte produces a new hash
questions.explanation: Hashes identify one exact file, so trivial modification defeats them.

questions.question: Why must scope be established before remediation?
options: Cleaning one host while the attacker retains access elsewhere achieves nothing
questions.explanation: Partial remediation alerts the attacker while leaving their access intact.

questions.question: What is the first step in malware incident response?
options: Isolate the host from the network while preserving evidence
questions.explanation: Isolation stops spread and attacker communication without destroying volatile evidence.

questions.question: What is the critical design rule for AI-integrated applications?
options: Model output must not directly trigger privileged actions
questions.explanation: If output can cause privileged action, anyone influencing input can cause it too.

questions.question: What should be confirmed before sending data to a managed AI service?
options: Retention terms and whether inputs are used for training
questions.explanation: Data handling terms determine whether submission constitutes an unacceptable disclosure.

questions.question: What does 'defence in depth' mean?
options: Layering several independent controls so one failure is not fatal
questions.explanation: Multiple independent layers mean an attacker who defeats one control still faces others.

questions.question: Which port does HTTPS use by default?
questions.explanation: HTTPS uses TCP port 443, while unencrypted HTTP uses port 80.

questions.question: What is the difference between a policy and a procedure?
options: A policy states requirements; a procedure states the steps
A procedure is approved by management
questions.explanation: Policies define what must be achieved; procedures describe how to achieve it.

questions.question: Which command lists current network connections with their owning processes?
questions.explanation: ss with those flags shows established connections alongside the processes holding them.

questions.question: Why must security decisions be enforced server-side?
options: Anything enforced in the browser can be altered by the user
questions.explanation: Client-side controls are advisory because the client is under the user's control.

questions.question: What does a CSRF attack achieve?
options: Causing the victim's browser to perform an action on a site where they are logged in
questions.explanation: The attacker cannot read the response; CSRF causes unintended state-changing actions.

questions.question: Where should an API key be stored?
options: In an environment variable or secrets manager
questions.explanation: Keys in source code are exposed through version control and are found by automated scanners.

questions.question: Why does a 99% accurate model still produce many false positives?
options: Almost all events are benign, so even a small error rate is a large number
questions.explanation: At very low base rates the volume of benign events dominates the error count.
